Identities and periodic oscillations of divide-and-conquer recurrences splitting at half

The work of the first author was partially supported by National Science and Technology Council under the Grant MOST-108-2118-M-001-005-MY3, and part of it was carried out while he was visiting Department of Mathematics, Uppsala University; he thanks the Department for hospitality and support. Part of the work of the second author was carried out during visits to the Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences (EPSCR Grant Number EP/K032208/1) and was partially supported by a grant from the Simons Foundation, and a grant from the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation; he thanks these for hospitality and support.
Hsien-Kuei Hwang Affiliation: Institute of Statistical Science, Affiliation: Academia Sinica Affiliation: Taipei 115 Affiliation: Taiwan    Svante Janson Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: Uppsala University Affiliation: Uppsala Affiliation: Sweden    Tsung-Hsi Tsai Affiliation: Institute of Statistical Science Affiliation: Academia Sinica Affiliation: Taipei 115 Affiliation: Taiwan
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We study divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form

f⁡(n)=α​f​(⌊n2⌋)+β​f​(⌈n2⌉)+g⁡(n)(n⩾2),f(n)=\alpha f\bigl({\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\bigr\rfloor}\bigr)+\beta f\bigl({\bigl\lceil\tfrac{n}{2}\bigr\rceil}\bigr)+g(n)\qquad(n\geqslant 2),

with g⁡(n)g(n) and f⁡(1)f(1) given, where α,β⩾0\alpha,\beta\geqslant 0 with α+β>0\alpha+\beta>0; such recurrences appear often in analysis of computer algorithms, numeration systems, combinatorial sequences, and related areas. We show that the solution satisfies always the simple identity

f⁡(n)=nlog2⁡(α+β)​P​(log2⁡n)−Q⁡(n)f(n)=n^{\log_{2}(\alpha+\beta)}P(\log_{2}n)-Q(n)

under an optimum (iff) condition on g⁡(n)g(n). This form is not only an identity but also an asymptotic expansion because Q⁡(n)Q(n) is of a smaller order. Explicit forms for the continuity of the periodic function PP are provided, together with a few other smoothness properties. We show how our results can be easily applied to many dozens of concrete examples collected from the literature, and how they can be extended in various directions. Our method of proof is surprisingly simple and elementary, but leads to the strongest types of results for all examples to which our theory applies.

1 Introduction

This paper is a sequel to [27], where we studied the case (α,β)=(1,1)(\alpha,\beta)=(1,1) of the following recurrence

f⁡(n)=α​f​(⌊n2⌋)+β​f​(⌈n2⌉)+g⁡(n)(n⩾2),f(n)=\alpha f\bigl({\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\bigr\rfloor}\bigr)+\beta f\bigl({\bigl\lceil\tfrac{n}{2}\bigr\rceil}\bigr)+g(n)\qquad(n\geqslant 2), (1.1)

with f⁡(1)f(1) and {g⁡(n)}n⩾2\{g(n)\}_{n\geqslant 2} given; we focus here on the general case of two given constants α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0. (The case when α⩽0\alpha\leqslant 0 or β⩽0\beta\leqslant 0 is briefly discussed in Section 6.) As in [27], our aim in this paper will be

  • •

    to establish optimum iff-conditions for the identity

    f⁡(n)=nϱ​P​(log2⁡n)−Q⁡(n)(n⩾1),f(n)=n^{\varrho}P(\log_{2}n)-Q(n)\qquad(n\geqslant 1), (1.2)

    which is also an asymptotic expansion, where

    ϱ:=log2⁡(α+β),\displaystyle\varrho:=\log_{2}(\alpha+\beta), (1.3)

    PP is a bounded, continuous, periodic function and Q⁡(n)Q(n) is of a smaller order o⁡(nϱ)o(n^{\varrho}); and

  • •

    to explore the usefulness of such a result by examining other associated properties and applying to many concrete examples.

In addition, we also examine further smoothness properties of the periodic function PP, and introduce and explore a new notion to describe the equivalence of different recurrences.

An elementary interpolation approach.

The crucial step of our approach is to identify a (generally nonlinear) interpolation function φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) such that the sequence f⁡(n)f(n) as defined by (1.1) for positive integers nn can be extended to a continuous function f⁡(x)f(x) defined for all real x⩾1x\geqslant 1 in the way that f⁡(x)f(x) equals the original sequence f⁡(n)f(n) when x=nx=n, a positive integer, and there is a version of the recurrence (1.1) valid for all xx; see Section 2 for details.

Such an interpolation-based analysis for (1.1) will then be extended (in Section 7) to the more general qq-ary recurrence (q⩾2q\geqslant 2) of the form

f⁡(n)=∑0⩽j<qαj​f​(⌊n+jq⌋)+g⁡(n)(n⩾q),f(n)=\sum_{0\leqslant j<q}\alpha_{j}f\bigl({\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{n+j}{q}\bigr\rfloor}\bigr)+g(n)\qquad(n\geqslant q), (1.4)

for some given constants α0,…,αq−1\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{q-1}, and a result of the form (1.2) will also be derived under some conditions. Typical situations where (1.4) arises is the application of divide-and-conquer into qq parts whose sizes are as evenly as possible. The special case when αj=1\alpha_{j}=1 for 0⩽j<q0\leqslant j<q was already discussed in [27]. Another special case is αj=0\alpha_{j}=0 for 1⩽j⩽q−21\leqslant j\leqslant q-2, which yields (with α=α0\alpha=\alpha_{0} and β=αq−1\beta=\alpha_{q-1}) the recursion f⁡(n)=α​f​(⌊nq⌋)+β​f​(⌈nq⌉)+g⁡(n)f(n)=\alpha f(\lfloor\frac{n}{q}\rfloor)+\beta f(\lceil\frac{n}{q}\rceil)+g(n) considered in [11, Theorem 4.1] and [33] although they allow also non-integer q>1q>1.

Recurrences with or without floors and ceilings.

While the divide-and-conquer paradigm with evenly divided parts is widely used in computer algorithms, our formulation of the divide-and-conquer recurrence (1.4), as well as the very precise identity (1.2), is surprisingly rare in the computer algorithm literature; instead one finds predominantly a recurrence of the form

f⁡(n)=(α+β)​f​(n2)+g⁡(n),\displaystyle f(n)=(\alpha+\beta)f\bigl({\tfrac{n}{2}}\bigr)+g(n), (1.5)

or more generally

f⁡(n)=∑0⩽j<dαj​f​(nqj)+g⁡(n),\displaystyle f(n)=\sum_{0\leqslant j<d}\alpha_{j}f\bigl({\tfrac{n}{q_{j}}}\bigr)+g(n), (1.6)

where α,αj>0\alpha,\alpha_{j}>0, d=1,2,…d=1,2,\dots and qj>1q_{j}>1. According to the first edition of Cormen et al.’s widely used textbook on Algorithms [10, p. 54]: “When we state and solve recurrences, we often omit floors, ceilings, and boundary conditions. We forge ahead without these details and later determine whether or not they matter. …we shall address some of these details to show the fine points of recurrence solution methods.”

Such a simplifying approach also appears in most publications on Algorithms. One of our aims in this paper is to show that retaining floors and ceilings is not much more complicated than omitting them, and with various advantages that are mostly unnoticed in the literature. This suggests that one main reason of omitting floors and ceilings in handling a divide-and-conquer recurrence lies more in methodological deficiencies than simply technical conventions; the approach proposed in this paper will then complete to some extent the required methodological developments.

More precisely, when α,β,g⁡(n)⩾0\alpha,\beta,g(n)\geqslant 0, typical approaches adopted in the computer algorithms community to solving the recurrence (1.1) include

  • •

    dropping floor and ceiling in (1.1) by assuming nn to be a power of 22, resulting in the closed-form expression

    f⁡(2m)=∑1⩽j⩽m(α+β)m−j​g​(2j)+(α+β)m​f​(1),\displaystyle f(2^{m})=\sum_{1\leqslant j\leqslant m}(\alpha+\beta)^{m-j}g(2^{j})+(\alpha+\beta)^{m}f(1), (1.7)

    and

  • •

    lower- and upper-bounding ff by keeping only floor and only ceiling function in (1.1), leading to

    f−​(n):=(α+β)​f−​(⌊n2⌋)+g⁡(n),\displaystyle f_{-}(n):=(\alpha+\beta)f_{-}\bigl({\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor}\bigr)+g(n), (1.8)

    and

    f+​(n):=(α+β)​f+​(⌈n2⌉)+g⁡(n),\displaystyle f_{+}(n):=(\alpha+\beta)f_{+}\bigl({\lceil\tfrac{n}{2}\rceil}\bigr)+g(n), (1.9)

    respectively.

While simple and effective in estimating the growth order of f⁡(n)f(n) for large nn, both approaches suffer from subtle oversights and intrinsic limitations, with different shortcomings.

Monotonicity.

First, in either of the approaches (1.7) and (1.8)–(1.9), the next crucial property used in estimating the asymptotic growth of f⁡(n)f(n) is monotonicity, which in the first approach is of the form f⁡(2m)⩽f⁡(2m+ℓ)⩽f⁡(2m+1)f(2^{m})\leqslant f(2^{m}+\ell)\leqslant f(2^{m+1}) for 0⩽ℓ⩽2m0\leqslant\ell\leqslant 2^{m}, and f−​(n)⩽f⁡(n)⩽f+​(n)f_{-}(n)\leqslant f(n)\leqslant f_{+}(n) in the second approach. However, these inequalities may not hold in general due to the periodic nature of the recurrences (1.1), (1.8) and (1.9). For example, take α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1 and g⁡(n)=1+𝟏n​ oddg(n)=1+\mathbf{1}_{n\text{ odd}} with f⁡(1)=f+​(1)=0f(1)=f_{+}(1)=0. Then 8=f⁡(7)>f⁡(8)=78=f(7)>f(8)=7, and f⁡(15)=17>f+​(15)=16f(15)=17>f_{+}(15)=16. Thus the use of the monotonicity is more subtle than it is generally taken to be.

On the other hand, when g⁡(n)=𝟏n​ oddg(n)=\mathbf{1}_{n\text{ odd}} with f⁡(1)=0f(1)=0 (which yields A296062 in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences database [34] with many combinatorial interpretations), then f⁡(n)f(n) oscillates between 00 and Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n). Thus not only monotonicity fails but also the growth order oscillates violently, although our result yields that f⁡(n)=n​P​(log2⁡n)f(n)=nP(\log_{2}n) for some continuous periodic function; see (5.7).

Discontinuity.

Apart from monotonicity, there is yet another deeper reason why the original sequence (1.1) is preferred to its simplified one-sided versions (1.8) and (1.9): the periodic function PP in (1.2) is always continuous, while the corresponding one for the solution of either (1.8) or (1.9) is almost always discontinuous; more precisely, in typical cases the function P⁡(t)P(t) is discontinuous at every tt such that 2t2^{t} is a dyadic rational, i.e., has a finite binary representation (see Section 6.1 and, for details in the case α+β=2\alpha+\beta=2, [27, Section 8]). But why does continuity matters here? The reason is because the periodic function PP when evaluated at log2⁡n\log_{2}n (see (1.2)), involves indeed functions evaluated at the dyadic rational n/2⌊log2⁡n⌋n/2^{\lfloor\log_{2}n\rfloor} (see (2.22) and (2.30)), so that discontinuity causes the sequence (or the original cost function) to have more violent jumps even for neighbouring input sizes. Thus simplifying the recurrence (1.1) to either (1.8) or (1.9) has the advantage of being easily solvable by iteration, but suffers from structural discontinuities, or more rough oscillations.

Master theorems.

Another commonly used approach to solve (1.5) is to apply the so-called “master theorems” (see [2, 11]), which are generally effective and user-friendly, but does not provide more precise asymptotic approximations. For example, in the case of (1.1), if g⁡(n)=O⁡(nϱ−ε)g(n)=O(n^{\varrho-\varepsilon}), ε>0\varepsilon>0, then the master theorem [11, § 4.5] or [33] gives f⁡(n)=Θ⁡(nϱ)f(n)=\Theta(n^{\varrho}), where ϱ\varrho is defined in (1.3), while under the same growth order of gg, our approach (see Corollary 2.14) again guarantees (1.2) with explicitly computable functions PP and QQ. There do exist finer master theorems that give more precise asymptotics under stronger assumptions on g⁡(n)g(n) (such as monotonicity; see [13]), but none of them is as precise as our identity (1.2).

Discrete and continuous master theorems.

An additional feature of our interpolation-based analysis is that we always work on the same real function f⁡(x)f(x), which coincides with the original sequence f⁡(n)f(n) at integer parameters, unlike general master theorems that distinguish between “discrete master theorems” and “continuous master theorems”; for example, according to [33]:

To distinguish the two situations, we call the master theorem without floors and ceilings the continuous master theorem and the master theorem with floors and ceilings the discrete master theorem.

The subtleties of the two different versions (together with other issues) are only very recently thoroughly examined in [33], where they write:

Several academic works provide proofs and proof sketches of the discrete master theorem. To the best of our knowledge, however, all of these proofs are either incomplete, incorrect, or require sophisticated mathematics.

See also the long paper (more than 300 pages) [4] for other delicate issues arising from divide-and-conquer recurrences. Additionally, the chapter on “Recurrences” (Chapter I.4) in the first edition of Cormen et al.’s book [10] is now largely expanded and updated in the latest, very recent, edition [11, Ch. I.4], more than three decades after its first edition and following the corresponding developments in clarifying the subtleties; see [4, 11].

For more information and references on master theorems and divide-and-conquer recurrences, see, for example, [13, 23, 26, 33, 35]. See also [27] for more references on other approaches (including complex-analytic, Tauberian, renewal, fractal geometry, and Ansatz or guess-and-prove, called the substitution method in [11]) used in the literature for solving (1.1).

Periodic equivalence of sequences.

For a more canonical way to group or classify the diverse periodic functions PP, we will introduce in Section 4.1 a useful notion called “periodic equivalence”, roughly meaning that different sequences share, modulo amplitude and scale, the same oscillating part. For example, denote by S2,1​(n)S_{2,1}(n) (A006046) the total number of odd entries in the first nn rows of Pascal triangle; then f​(n)=S2,1​(n)f(n)=S_{2,1}(n) satisfies (1.1) with (α,β)=(2,1)(\alpha,\beta)=(2,1), g⁡(n)=0g(n)=0 and f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1. We have S2,1​(n)=nlog2⁡3​P​(log2⁡n)S_{2,1}(n)=n^{\log_{2}3}P(\log_{2}n); see Example 4.9. Then the following OEIS sequences, all satisfying (1.1) with (α,β)=(2,1)(\alpha,\beta)=(2,1), are periodically equivalent to S2,1​(n)S_{2,1}(n) (involving, up to scale and amplitude, the same PP):

Smoothness of the periodic function.

While the periodic equivalence is introduced to identify the same fluctuating part of different sequences satisfying the same recurrence, we also examine the varying smoothness nature exhibited by different recurrences. The main motivating observation is that most periodic functions we obtain have visible cusps (likely to be non-differentiable points), and there are other classes of functions (such as Lipshitz and Hölder continuous) between the class of continuous functions and that of continuously differentiable functions. We will thus clarify the different, characteristic, inherent types of Hölder continuity of the interpolated function f⁡(x)f(x) and the periodic function P⁡(t)P(t) when (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) varies.

For example, in Figure 1, we plot the periodic functions PP (as defined in (1.2)) when ff satisfies (1.1) with g⁡(n)=0g(n)=0 and f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1, and with (α,β)=(α,1)(\alpha,\beta)=(\alpha,1), α=2,3,4,5\alpha=2,3,4,5 (the lower blue curves) and (α,β)=(1,β)(\alpha,\beta)=(1,\beta), β=2,3,4,5\beta=2,3,4,5 (the upper green curves). Our results show that these periodic functions are Hölder continuous with exponent log2⁡(1+α−1)\log_{2}(1+\alpha^{-1}) and log2⁡(1+β−1)\log_{2}(1+\beta^{-1}), respectively, and we conjecture that these exponents are the best possible; see Section 3 for details. Thus for these recurrences, the larger the values of α\alpha or β\beta, the “less smooth” the periodic functions.

Moreover, we show that many of the periodic functions appearing in our analysis are indeed not continuously differentiable at all points in (0,1)(0,1). Several examples are piecewise differentiable with jumps in the derivative at some points (see, for example, Remark 2.8 and Examples 5.4 and 5.5). Other examples are less smooth; for brevity of presentation, we discuss only one case (A006581) in detail in Example 5.6 and show (in Appendix D) that the periodic function is continuous but nowhere differentiable, leaving such a deeper property for other sequences to the interested reader.

A generating function viewpoint.

To see how the general cases differ from the special case (α,β)=(1,1)(\alpha,\beta)=(1,1) or more generally α=β\alpha=\beta, we consider the generating function

A⁡(z):=∑n⩾1f⁡(n)​zn,A(z):=\sum_{n\geqslant 1}f(n)z^{n}, (1.10)

which, by (1.1) satisfies the functional equation

A⁡(z)=β+(α+β)​z+α​z2z​A​(z2)+B⁡(z),A(z)=\frac{\beta+(\alpha+\beta)z+\alpha z^{2}}{z}\,A(z^{2})+B(z), (1.11)

where

B⁡(z):=f⁡(1)​(1−β)​z+∑n⩾2g⁡(n)​zn.B(z):=f(1)(1-\beta)z+\sum_{n\geqslant 2}g(n)z^{n}. (1.12)

We see that if α=β\alpha=\beta, then the functional equation becomes

A⁡(z)=α​(1+z)2z​A​(z2)+B⁡(z),A(z)=\frac{\alpha(1+z)^{2}}{z}\,A(z^{2})+B(z), (1.13)

so that the generating function A¯​(z):=(1−z)2z​A​(z)\bar{A}(z):=\frac{(1-z)^{2}}{z}\,A(z) of the second difference of f⁡(n)f(n) satisfies the simpler equation

A¯​(z)=α​A¯​(z2)+B¯​(z),\bar{A}(z)=\alpha\bar{A}(z^{2})+\bar{B}(z), (1.14)

where B¯​(z):=(1−z)2z​B​(z)\bar{B}(z):=\frac{(1-z)^{2}}{z}\,B(z). Assuming for simplicity (without real loss of generality) that B¯​(0)=0\bar{B}(0)=0, we then obtain, by iteration, the exact solution

A⁡(z)=z(1−z)2​∑k⩾0αk​B¯​(z2k).A(z)=\frac{z}{(1-z)^{2}}\sum_{k\geqslant 0}\alpha^{k}\bar{B}\bigl({z^{2^{k}}}\bigr). (1.15)

Such a neat representation is the basis of the analytic approach introduced in [20], but is not available in general when α≠β\alpha\neq\beta. We will therefore use a different method.

This paper is structured as follows. We develop in Section 2 the required technicalities in order to prove (1.2), and then address the smoothness properties of PP in Section 3. These two sections provide a theoretical foundation to the resolution of the divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form (1.1). Applications of our theory to concrete examples are discussed in Section 4 for α≠β\alpha\neq\beta and in Section 5 for α=β\alpha=\beta. We then extend very briefly our analysis to nonpositive α\alpha or β\beta in Section 6 and to general qq-ary recurrence (1.4) in Section 7. For completeness, an appendix on the connection of our approach to Mellin transforms is given, together with two others providing detailed proofs of some results in the paper.

Notation.

For convenience, we introduce the operator Λα,β\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta} as follows:

Λα,β​[f]​(n):=f⁡(n)−α​f​(⌊n2⌋)−β​f​(⌈n2⌉).\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f](n):=f(n)-\alpha f\left(\left\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\right\rfloor\right)-\beta f\left(\left\lceil\tfrac{n}{2}\right\rceil\right). (1.16)

Let, for x>0x>0,

Lx\displaystyle L_{x} :=⌊log2⁡x⌋,\displaystyle:=\left\lfloor\log_{2}x\right\rfloor, θx\displaystyle\theta_{x} :={log2⁡x}=log2⁡x−Lx∈[0,1),\displaystyle:=\{\log_{2}x\}=\log_{2}x-L_{x}\in[0,1), (1.17)

and L0:=0L_{0}:=0.

For real xx and yy, we let x∨y:=max⁡(x,y)x\vee y:=\max(x,y).

2 The recurrence Λα,β​[f]=g\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f]=g

Here and throughout this section, we assume that α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, and define g⁡(1):=0g(1):=0. The recurrence (1.1) can be rewritten as

f⁡(2​n)=(α+β)​f​(n)+g⁡(2​n),f⁡(2​n+1)=α​f​(n)+β​f​(n+1)+g⁡(2​n+1),\begin{split}f(2n)&=(\alpha+\beta)f(n)+g(2n),\\ f(2n+1)&=\alpha f(n)+\beta f(n+1)+g(2n+1),\end{split} (2.1)

for n⩾1n\geqslant 1, with given f⁡(1)f(1) and g⁡(n)g(n), n⩾2n\geqslant 2.

Extending the sequence f⁡(n)f(n) to a function f⁡(x)f(x) in ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{+}.

We extend the sequence f⁡(n)f(n) to a continuous function f⁡(x)f(x) defined for real x⩾1x\geqslant 1 by interpolation between the integers with scaled copies of a certain function φ:[0,1]→[0,1]\varphi:[0,1]\to[0,1] constructed below:

f⁡(n+t)\displaystyle f(n+t) :=f⁡(n)+φ⁡(t)​(f⁡(n+1)−f⁡(n))\displaystyle:=f(n)+\varphi(t)\left(f(n+1)-f(n)\right)
=(1−φ⁡(t))​f​(n)+φ⁡(t)​f​(n+1),\displaystyle=\left(1-\varphi(t)\right)f\left(n\right)+\varphi(t)f\left(n+1\right), (2.2)

for n⩾1n\geqslant 1 and 0⩽t⩽10\leqslant t\leqslant 1; in a similar way, we construct g⁡(x)g(x) from g⁡(n)g(n). The function φ\varphi is constructed so that we will have

f⁡(x)=(α+β)​f​(x2)+g⁡(x),x⩾2.f(x)=(\alpha+\beta)f\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)+g(x),\qquad x\geqslant 2. (2.3)

We further define g⁡(x):=0g(x):=0 for x∈[0,1)x\in[0,1); thus g⁡(x)g(x) is defined for x⩾0x\geqslant 0.

The function φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) depends on α\alpha and β\beta; we sometimes write it as φα,β​(t)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(t) to emphasise the dependence on parameters.

Construction of the interpolation function φ\varphi.

We first give relations on φ\varphi that imply the functional equation (2.3). The existence of such a φ\varphi is shown later.

Lemma 2.1.

Let φ​(t)=φα,β​(t)\varphi(t)=\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(t) be a function on [0,1][0,1] such that φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0, φ⁡(1)=1\varphi(1)=1 and

φ⁡(t)={βα+β​φ​(2​t),if ​t∈[0,12],αα+β​φ​(2​t−1)+βα+β,if ​t∈[12,1].\varphi(t)=\begin{cases}\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\,\varphi(2t),&\text{if\/ }t\in[0,\frac{1}{2}],\\ \tfrac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\,\varphi(2t-1)+\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta},&\text{if\/ }t\in[\frac{1}{2},1].\end{cases} (2.4)

Assume that (2.1) holds. Then (2.3) holds if we extend f⁡(n)f(n) and g⁡(n)g(n) by (2.2) to f⁡(x)f(x) and g⁡(x)g(x), respectively, for all real x⩾1x\geqslant 1.

Proof.

If n⩾1n\geqslant 1 and 0⩽t⩽120\leqslant t\leqslant\frac{1}{2}, then, using the interpolation (2.2), the recurrences (2.1) and the assumption (2.4), we have

f⁡(2​n+2​t)−g⁡(2​n+2​t)\displaystyle f(2n+2t)-g(2n+2t)
=(1−φ⁡(2​t))​(f⁡(2​n)−g⁡(2​n))+φ⁡(2​t)​(f⁡(2​n+1)−g⁡(2​n+1))\displaystyle=(1-\varphi(2t))(f(2n)-g(2n))+\varphi(2t)(f(2n+1)-g(2n+1))
=(1−φ⁡(2​t))​(α+β)​f​(n)+φ⁡(2​t)​(α​f​(n)+β​f​(n+1))\displaystyle=(1-\varphi(2t))(\alpha+\beta)f(n)+\varphi(2t)\bigl(\alpha f(n)+\beta f(n+1)\bigr)
=(α+β)​f​(n)−φ⁡(2​t)​β​f​(n)+φ⁡(2​t)​β​f​(n+1)\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)f(n)-\varphi(2t)\beta f(n)+\varphi(2t)\beta f(n+1)
=(α+β)​f​(n)−(α+β)​φ​(t)​f​(n)+(α+β)​φ​(t)​f​(n+1)\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)f(n)-(\alpha+\beta)\varphi(t)f(n)+(\alpha+\beta)\varphi(t)f(n+1)
=(α+β)​((1−φ⁡(t))​f​(n)+φ⁡(t)​f​(n+1))\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)\bigl((1-\varphi(t))f(n)+\varphi(t)f(n+1)\bigr)
=(α+β)​f​(n+t).\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)f(n+t). (2.5)

Similarly, the lower part of (2.4) can be rewritten as

(α+β)​φ​(12+t)=α​φ​(2​t)+β,t∈[0,12],\displaystyle(\alpha+\beta)\,\varphi\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+t\right)=\alpha\varphi(2t)+\beta,\qquad t\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}], (2.6)

and thus, still for n⩾1n\geqslant 1 and 0⩽t⩽120\leqslant t\leqslant\frac{1}{2},

f⁡(2​n+1+2​t)−g⁡(2​n+1+2​t)\displaystyle f(2n+1+2t)-g(2n+1+2t)
=(1−φ⁡(2​t))​(f⁡(2​n+1)−g⁡(2​n+1))+φ⁡(2​t)​(f⁡(2​n+2)−g⁡(2​n+2))\displaystyle=(1-\varphi(2t))(f(2n+1)-g(2n+1))+\varphi(2t)(f(2n+2)-g(2n+2))
=(1−φ⁡(2​t))​(α​f​(n)+β​f​(n+1))+φ⁡(2​t)​(α+β)​f​(n+1)\displaystyle=(1-\varphi(2t))(\alpha f(n)+\beta f(n+1))+\varphi(2t)(\alpha+\beta)f(n+1)
=α​f​(n)+β​f​(n+1)−φ⁡(2​t)​α​f​(n)+φ⁡(2​t)​α​f​(n+1)\displaystyle=\alpha f(n)+\beta f(n+1)-\varphi(2t)\alpha f(n)+\varphi(2t)\alpha f(n+1)
=α​f​(n)+β​f​(n+1)−((α+β)​φ​(12+t)−β)​(f⁡(n)−f⁡(n+1))\displaystyle=\alpha f(n)+\beta f(n+1)-\left((\alpha+\beta)\varphi\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+t\right)-\beta\right)\bigl(f(n)-f(n+1)\bigr)
=(α+β)​f​(n)−(α+β)​φ​(12+t)​f​(n)+(α+β)​φ​(12+t)​f​(n+1)\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)f(n)-(\alpha+\beta)\varphi\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+t\right)f(n)+(\alpha+\beta)\varphi\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+t\right)f(n+1)
=(α+β)​((1−φ⁡(12+t))​f​(n)+φ⁡(12+t)​f​(n+1))\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)\left(\left(1-\varphi\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+t\right)\right)f(n)+\varphi\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+t\right)f(n+1)\right)
=(α+β)​f​(n+12+t).\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)f\left(n+\tfrac{1}{2}+t\right). (2.7)

Combining (2.5) and (2.7), we obtain

f⁡(n+2​t)=(α+β)​f​(n2+t)+g⁡(n+2​t)f(n+2t)=(\alpha+\beta)f\left(\tfrac{n}{2}+t\right)+g(n+2t) (2.8)

for n⩾2n\geqslant 2 and 0⩽t⩽120\leqslant t\leqslant\frac{1}{2}, and thus (2.3) holds. ∎

Remark 2.2.

Conversely, it is immediate that if (2.3) holds for the extensions of ff and gg defined by (2.2), then (2.1) holds.

In the case α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1 treated in [27], the system of equations (2.4) has the solution φ⁡(t)=t\varphi(t)=t. In general, it is not obvious that a continuous solution to (2.4) exists. We now show that this is the case, and that this φ\varphi is unique.

Lemma 2.3.

If α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, then there exists a unique continuous function φ​(t)=φα,β​(t)\varphi(t)=\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(t) on [0,1][0,1] such that φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0, φ⁡(1)=1\varphi(1)=1 and (2.4) holds. Moreover, φ\varphi is strictly increasing.

Proof.

The equation (2.4) and the conditions φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0, φ⁡(1)=1\varphi(1)=1 define recursively φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) uniquely for dyadic rational t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]; hence, there is at most one continuous φ\varphi satisfying these requirements. The existence of such a φ\varphi can be proved in several different ways.

First proof (probabilistic).

Let φ\varphi be the distribution function φ⁡(t):=Pr⁡(X⩽t)\varphi(t):=\Pr(X\leqslant t) of the random variable X∈[0,1]X\in[0,1] defined by the binary expansion X=0.B1​B2​…X=0.B_{1}B_{2}\dots, where the bits B1,B2,…B_{1},B_{2},\dots are independent and with Pr⁡(Bi=1)=αα+β\Pr(B_{i}=1)=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}. Since the random variable X′:=0.B2​B3​⋯=2​X−B1X^{\prime}:=0.B_{2}B_{3}\dots=2X-B_{1} has the same distribution as XX, we see that

φ⁡(t):=Pr⁡(X⩽t)={Pr⁡(B1=0)​Pr⁡(X′⩽2​t),t∈[0,12],Pr⁡(B1=0)+Pr⁡(B1=1)​Pr⁡(X′⩽2​t−1),t∈[12,1],={βα+β​φ​(2​t),t∈[0,12],βα+β+αα+β​φ​(2​t−1),t∈[12,1],\begin{split}\varphi(t)&:=\Pr(X\leqslant t)\\ &=\begin{cases}\Pr(B_{1}=0)\Pr(X^{\prime}\leqslant 2t),&t\in[0,\frac{1}{2}],\\ \Pr(B_{1}=0)+\Pr(B_{1}=1)\Pr(X^{\prime}\leqslant 2t-1),&t\in[\frac{1}{2},1],\end{cases}\\ &=\begin{cases}\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\,\varphi(2t),&t\in[0,\frac{1}{2}],\\ \frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}+\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\,\varphi(2t-1),&t\in[\frac{1}{2},1],\end{cases}\end{split} (2.9)

which verifies (2.4). Furthermore, φ\varphi is continuous and strictly increasing on [0,1][0,1], with φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0 and φ⁡(1)=1\varphi(1)=1.

Second proof (digital sums).

An alternative approach begins with an explicit construction, which will also be useful later. For t=∑j⩾1bj​2−j∈[0,1]t=\sum_{j\geqslant 1}b_{j}2^{-j}\in[0,1], where bj∈{0,1}b_{j}\in\{0,1\}, define

φ⁡(t):=∑j⩾1bj​(αβ)b1+⋯+bj−1​(βα+β)j.\displaystyle\varphi(t):=\sum_{j\geqslant 1}b_{j}\left(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right)^{b_{1}+\cdots+b_{j-1}}\biggl(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\biggr)^{j}. (2.10)

Equivalently, define, for t=∑k⩾12−ek∈[0,1]t=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}2^{-e_{k}}\in[0,1], where 1⩽e1<e2<⋯1\leqslant e_{1}<e_{2}<\cdots is a finite or infinite sequence,

φ⁡(t=∑k⩾12−ek):=∑k⩾1αk−1​βek−k+1(α+β)ek.\varphi\biggl(t=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}2^{-e_{k}}\biggr):=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}\frac{\alpha^{k-1}\beta^{e_{k}-k+1}}{\left(\alpha+\beta\right)^{e_{k}}}. (2.11)

We first show that both (2.10) and (2.11) are well defined for dyadic rational tt with two different representations, namely,

∑1⩽i⩽k2−ei=∑1⩽j<k2−ej+∑j⩾12−(ek+j).\displaystyle\sum_{1\leqslant i\leqslant k}2^{-e_{i}}=\sum_{1\leqslant j<k}2^{-e_{j}}+\sum_{j\geqslant 1}2^{-(e_{k}+j)}. (2.12)

The value in (2.11) for the last term on the left-hand side of (2.12) is αk−1​βek−k+1(α+β)ek\frac{\alpha^{k-1}\beta^{e_{k}-k+1}}{\left(\alpha+\beta\right)^{e_{k}}}; the value for the sum on the right-hand side equals

∑j⩾1α(k+j−1)−1​βek+j−(k+j−1)+1(α+β)ek+j=αk−1​βek−k+1(α+β)ek​∑j⩾1αj−1​β(α+β)j=αk−1​βek−k+1(α+β)ek,\sum_{j\geqslant 1}\frac{\alpha^{(k+j-1)-1}\beta^{e_{k}+j-(k+j-1)+1}}{(\alpha+\beta)^{e_{k}+j}}=\frac{\alpha^{k-1}\beta^{e_{k}-k+1}}{(\alpha+\beta)^{e_{k}}}\sum_{j\geqslant 1}\frac{\alpha^{j-1}\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^{j}}=\frac{\alpha^{k-1}\beta^{e_{k}-k+1}}{(\alpha+\beta)^{e_{k}}}, (2.13)

since the final geometric series sums to 1. Hence, the two representations in (2.12) yield the same sum (2.11), which always equals the sum (2.10), and thus φ\varphi is well-defined on [0,1][0,1].

Clearly, φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0 and φ⁡(1)=1\varphi(1)=1, again by summing the same geometric sum. Moreover, (2.4) follows easily from (2.10), considering the cases b1=0b_{1}=0 and b1=1b_{1}=1 separately.

Next, if t=∑1⩽j⩽Nbj​2−jt=\sum_{1\leqslant j\leqslant N}b_{j}2^{-j} is a dyadic rational in [0,1)[0,1), and s:=∑1⩽j⩽Nbjs:=\sum_{1\leqslant j\leqslant N}b_{j}, then, by (2.4) and induction on N⩾0N\geqslant 0, we have

φ⁡(t+2−N)−φ⁡(t)=αs​βN−s(α+β)N.\displaystyle\varphi\bigl(t+2^{-N}\bigr)-\varphi(t)=\frac{\alpha^{s}\beta^{N-s}}{(\alpha+\beta)^{N}}. (2.14)

It follows from (2.14) that φ\varphi is strictly increasing on the set of dyadic rationals in [0,1][0,1]. Furthermore, suppose that t1=j​2−Nt_{1}=j2^{-N} is a dyadic rational in [0,1)[0,1), and let t2:=t+2−Nt_{2}:=t+2^{-N}. If t∈[t1,t2]t\in[t_{1},t_{2}], then both tt and t2t_{2} have binary expansions beginning with the expansion of t1t_{1} (choosing the infinite representation for t2t_{2}), and it follows from (2.11) that φ⁡(t1)⩽φ⁡(t)⩽φ⁡(t2)\varphi(t_{1})\leqslant\varphi(t)\leqslant\varphi(t_{2}). Now, suppose 0⩽t<u⩽10\leqslant t<u\leqslant 1, and choose NN such that 21−N<u−t2^{1-N}<u-t. Then there exist jj and kk with j​2−N⩽t⩽(j+1)​2−N<k​2−N⩽u⩽(k+1)​2−Nj2^{-N}\leqslant t\leqslant(j+1)2^{-N}<k2^{-N}\leqslant u\leqslant(k+1)2^{-N}. Hence, by what was just shown, φ⁡(t)⩽φ⁡((j+1)​2−N)<φ⁡(k​2−N)⩽φ⁡(u)\varphi(t)\leqslant\varphi\bigl((j+1)2^{-N}\bigr)<\varphi\bigl(k2^{-N}\bigr)\leqslant\varphi(u). Thus, φ\varphi is strictly increasing.

The monotonicity implies that any discontinuity of φ\varphi must be a jump. Define

Δ+​φ​(t):=limu↘tφ⁡(u)−φ⁡(t),t∈[0,1),\displaystyle\Delta_{+}\varphi(t):=\lim_{u\searrow t}\varphi(u)-\varphi(t),\qquad t\in[0,1), (2.15)

the jump to the right at tt, and let R:=supt∈[0,1)Δ+​(t)R:=\sup_{t\in[0,1)}\Delta_{+}(t). It follows from (2.4) that R=α∨βα+β​RR=\frac{{\alpha\lor\beta}}{\alpha+\beta}R, and thus R=0R=0. Hence, φ\varphi is right-continuous. Similarly, φ\varphi is left-continuous.

Third proof (recursive construction).

Yet another alternative, similar to the construction of Koch’s snowflake curve [41], is to define φ0​(t):=t,t∈[0,1]\varphi_{0}(t):=t,t\in[0,1], and then recursively let φk+1\varphi_{k+1} consist of two suitably scaled copies of φk\varphi_{k}; more precisely

φk+1​(t):={βα+β​φk​(2​t),if ​t∈[0,12],αα+β​φk​(2​t−1)+βα+β,if ​t∈[12,1];\varphi_{k+1}(t):=\begin{cases}\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\,\varphi_{k}(2t),&\text{if }t\in[0,\frac{1}{2}],\\ \tfrac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\,\varphi_{k}(2t-1)+\tfrac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta},&\text{if }t\in[\frac{1}{2},1];\end{cases} (2.16)

see Figure 3 for an illustration. Then, by induction, |φk+1​(t)−φk​(t)|⩽(α∨βα+β)k|\varphi_{k+1}(t)-\varphi_{k}(t)|\leqslant\bigl(\frac{{\alpha\lor\beta}}{\alpha+\beta}\bigr)^{k} for k⩾0k\geqslant 0 and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]; consequently, the functions φk​(t)\varphi_{k}(t) converge uniformly on [0,1][0,1] to a continuous function φ\varphi satisfying (2.4), with φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0 and φ⁡(1)=1\varphi(1)=1. It follows also that φ\varphi is weakly increasing; it is then easy to show, using (2.4), that such φ\varphi is strictly increasing, but we omit this, since we have already shown this using the other constructions. ∎

Remark 2.4.

If α=β\alpha=\beta, then (2.4) is solved by φ⁡(t)=t\varphi(t)=t, just as in the case α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1 treated in [27], so f⁡(x)f(x) is defined in (2.2) by linear interpolation. If α≠β\alpha\neq\beta, then this is not the case; a linear interpolation would not yield (2.3).

Figure 2 shows that φ\varphi has a typical fractal shape when α≠β\alpha\neq\beta. We will show in Lemma 3.1 and Remark 3.5 below that φ\varphi is Hölder continuous but not Lipschitz continuous when α≠β\alpha\neq\beta.

Remark 2.5.

It follows from (2.4) that

φβ,α​(t)=1−φα,β​(1−t),\displaystyle\varphi_{\beta,\alpha}(t)=1-\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(1-t), (2.17)

so the graph of φβ,α\varphi_{\beta,\alpha} equals the graph of φα,β\varphi_{\alpha,\beta} rotated about (12,12)(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}). See Figures 2 and 3 for a graphical illustration of some examples.

Remark 2.6.

For later use we note that

∫01φ⁡(x)​𝑑x=βα+β.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\varphi(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}. (2.18)

To see this, we may denote the integral by II and integrate both sides of (2.4), which then yields

I=βα+β⋅12​I+αα+β⋅12​I+βα+β⋅12=12​I+12​βα+β;\displaystyle I=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\cdot\frac{1}{2}I+\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\cdot\frac{1}{2}I+\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}I+\frac{1}{2}\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}; (2.19)

solving II gives (2.18). ∎

Identities.

By iterating the functional equation (2.3), we obtain, for x⩾1x\geqslant 1,

f⁡(x)=∑0⩽k<m(α+β)k​g​(2−k​x)+(α+β)m​f​(2−m​x),0⩽m⩽Lx.f(x)=\sum_{0\leqslant k<m}(\alpha+\beta)^{k}g(2^{-k}x)+(\alpha+\beta)^{m}f(2^{-m}x),\qquad 0\leqslant m\leqslant L_{x}. (2.20)

This leads to the following identity.

Lemma 2.7.

Assume that ff satisfies (2.1) and (2.2). Then, for x⩾1x\geqslant 1,

x−ϱ​f​(x)=∑k⩾0(2−k​x)−ϱ​g​(2−k​x)+f⁡(1)​P0​(log2⁡x),x^{-\varrho}f(x)=\sum_{k\geqslant 0}(2^{-k}x)^{-\varrho}g(2^{-k}x)+f(1)P_{0}\left(\log_{2}x\right), (2.21)

where ϱ:=log2⁡(α+β)\varrho:=\log_{2}(\alpha+\beta) and

P0​(t):=(1+(α+β−1)​φ​(2{t}−1))​(α+β)−{t}P_{0}\left(t\right):=\left(1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi\bigl({2^{\{t\}}-1}\bigr)\right)(\alpha+\beta)^{-\{t\}} (2.22)

is a continuous 11-periodic function satisfying P0​(0)=P0​(1)=1P_{0}(0)=P_{0}(1)=1.

Since g⁡(x)=0g(x)=0 for x⩽1x\leqslant 1, the sum in (2.21) is indeed finite.

Proof.

First, (2.22) yields P0​(0)=1P_{0}(0)=1 and limt↗1P0​(t)=(1+(α+β−1)​φ​(1))​(α+β)−1=(α+β)​(α+β)−1=1=P0​(1)\lim_{t\nearrow 1}P_{0}(t)=\bigl(1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi(1)\bigr)(\alpha+\beta)^{-1}=(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta)^{-1}=1=P_{0}(1). Furthermore, P0P_{0} is continuous on [0,1)[0,1) since φ\varphi is continuous, and P0P_{0} is 11-periodic. It follows that P0P_{0} is continuous on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

By (2.1), f⁡(2)=(α+β)​f​(1)+g⁡(2)f(2)=\left(\alpha+\beta\right)f(1)+g(2). Thus, for 1⩽x<21\leqslant x<2, recalling g⁡(1)=0g(1)=0,

f⁡(x)\displaystyle f(x) =f⁡(1)+φ⁡(x−1)​(f⁡(2)−f⁡(1))\displaystyle=f(1)+\varphi(x-1)(f(2)-f(1))
=f⁡(1)+φ⁡(x−1)​((α+β−1)​f​(1)+g⁡(2))\displaystyle=f(1)+\varphi(x-1)\bigl((\alpha+\beta-1)f(1)+g(2)\bigr)
=f⁡(1)​(1+(α+β−1)​φ​(x−1))+g⁡(x)\displaystyle=f(1)\bigl(1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi(x-1)\bigr)+g(x)
=f⁡(1)​P0​(log2⁡x)​(α+β)log2⁡x+g⁡(x).\displaystyle=f(1)P_{0}\bigl(\log_{2}x\bigr)(\alpha+\beta)^{\log_{2}x}+g(x). (2.23)

Now consider x⩾1x\geqslant 1. Take m=Lxm=L_{x} in (2.20) and use (2.23) with xx replaced by 2−Lx​x=2θx∈[1,2)2^{-L_{x}}x=2^{\theta_{x}}\in[1,2); we then obtain, by the relation α+β=2ϱ\alpha+\beta=2^{\varrho},

f⁡(x)\displaystyle f(x) =∑0⩽k<Lx(α+β)k​g​(2−k​x)+(α+β)Lx​f​(2−Lx​x)\displaystyle=\sum_{0\leqslant k<L_{x}}(\alpha+\beta)^{k}g(2^{-k}x)+(\alpha+\beta)^{L_{x}}f(2^{-L_{x}}x)
=∑0⩽k⩽Lx(α+β)k​g​(2−k​x)+(α+β)Lx+θx​f​(1)​P0​(θx)\displaystyle=\sum_{0\leqslant k\leqslant L_{x}}(\alpha+\beta)^{k}g(2^{-k}x)+(\alpha+\beta)^{L_{x}+\theta_{x}}f(1)P_{0}\bigl(\theta_{x}\bigr)
=∑k⩾02ϱ​k​g​(2−k​x)+2ϱ​log2​x​f​(1)​P0​(log2⁡x).\displaystyle=\sum_{k\geqslant 0}2^{\varrho k}g(2^{-k}x)+2^{\varrho\log_{2}x}f(1)P_{0}\bigl(\log_{2}x\bigr). (2.24)

This implies (2.21). ∎

Remark 2.8.

If α=β\alpha=\beta, then φ⁡(t)=t\varphi(t)=t by Remark 2.4, and thus (2.22) yields

P0​(t):=(1+(α+β−1)​(2{t}−1))​(α+β)−{t}.P_{0}\left(t\right):=\bigl(1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\bigl({2^{\{t\}}-1}\bigr)\bigr)(\alpha+\beta)^{-\{t\}}. (2.25)

In the case α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1 studied in [27], and also in the case α=β=12\alpha=\beta=\frac{1}{2}, this yields P0​(t)≡1P_{0}(t)\equiv 1. In all other cases with α=β>0\alpha=\beta>0, the periodic function P0​(t)P_{0}(t) is infinitely differentiable in (0,1)(0,1), but a simple calculation shows that the derivative has a jump at the integers; hence, P0P_{0} is Lipschitz but not continuously differentiable.

Remark 2.9.

If β=1\beta=1, then (2.22) and (2.4) yield also

P0​(t)=(α+1)1−{t}​φ​(2{t}−1).\displaystyle P_{0}\left(t\right)=(\alpha+1)^{1-\{t\}}\varphi\bigl({2^{\{t\}-1}}\bigr). (2.26)

We can now give an extension of Theorem 2 in our previous paper [27].

Theorem 2.10.

Suppose that ff and gg are given by (2.1) and (2.2). The following are equivalent.

  1. (i)

    n−ϱ​f​(n)=P⁡(log2⁡n)+o⁡(1)n^{-\varrho}f(n)=P(\log_{2}n)+o(1) as n→∞n\to\infty, for some continuous 11-periodic function PP on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

  2. (ii)

    x−ϱ​f​(x)=P⁡(log2⁡x)+o⁡(1)x^{-\varrho}f(x)=P(\log_{2}x)+o(1) as x→∞x\to\infty, for some continuous 11-periodic function PP on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

  3. (iii)
    x−ϱ​f​(x)=P⁡(log2⁡x)+o⁡(1)as x→∞,\displaystyle x^{-\varrho}f(x)=P(\log_{2}x)+o(1)\qquad\text{as $x\to\infty$}, (2.27)

    for some 11-periodic function PP on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

  4. (iv)

    The sum

    Q⁡(x):=∑m⩾12−ϱ​m​g​(2m​x)\displaystyle Q(x):=\sum_{m\geqslant 1}2^{-\varrho m}g(2^{m}x) (2.28)

    converges uniformly for x∈[1,2]x\in[1,2].

Furthermore, when these conditions hold,

f⁡(x)=xϱ​P​(log2⁡x)−Q⁡(x),x⩾1,f(x)=x^{\varrho}P(\log_{2}x)-Q(x),\qquad x\geqslant 1, (2.29)

where Q⁡(x)=o⁡(xϱ)Q(x)=o(x^{\varrho}) as x→∞x\to\infty, Q⁡(x)Q(x) is defined by (2.28) for all x>0x>0, and the continuous periodic function P⁡(t)P(t) is given by

P⁡(t)=∑m∈ℤ2−ϱ⁡(m+t)​g​(2m+t)+f⁡(1)​P0​(t),t∈ℝ,P(t)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}2^{-\varrho(m+t)}g(2^{m+t})+f(1)P_{0}(t),\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}, (2.30)

with P0​(t)P_{0}(t) given by (2.22).

Note that (2.29) is not only an identity but also an asymptotic expansion.

Before proving Theorem 2.10, we give two partial results.

Proposition 2.11.

Suppose that h⁡(x)h(x) is a function such that h⁡(x)h(x) lies between h⁡(⌊x⌋)h\left(\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor\right) and h⁡(⌈x⌉)h\left(\left\lceil x\right\rceil\right). Then, the following are equivalent.

  1. (i)

    n−ϱ​h​(n)=P⁡(log2⁡n)+o⁡(1)n^{-\varrho}h(n)=P(\log_{2}n)+o(1) as n→∞n\to\infty, for some continuous 11-periodic function PP on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

  2. (ii)

    x−ϱ​h​(x)=P⁡(log2⁡x)+o⁡(1)x^{-\varrho}h(x)=P(\log_{2}x)+o(1) as x→∞x\to\infty, for some continuous 11-periodic function PP on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

(ii)⟹\implies(i) is trivial.

The proof of (i)⟹\implies(ii) is very similar to the proof of (i)⟹\implies(ii) in [27, Theorem 2], so we omit some details. First, log2⁡x−log2⁡⌊x⌋=O⁡(1/x)=o⁡(1)\log_{2}x-\log_{2}\lfloor x\rfloor=O(1/x)=o(1) for large xx and PP is uniformly continuous, so P⁡(log2⁡x)=P⁡(log2⁡⌊x⌋)+o⁡(1)P(\log_{2}x)=P\bigl(\log_{2}\lfloor x\rfloor\bigr)+o(1). Hence, (i) implies that

⌊x⌋−ϱ​h​(⌊x⌋)=P⁡(log2⁡⌊x⌋)+o⁡(1)=P⁡(log2⁡x)+o⁡(1)\displaystyle\lfloor x\rfloor^{-\varrho}h\bigl(\lfloor x\rfloor\bigr)=P\bigl(\log_{2}\lfloor x\rfloor\bigr)+o(1)=P\bigl(\log_{2}{x}\bigr)+o(1) (2.31)

and consequently, x−ϱ​h​(⌊x⌋)=P⁡(log2⁡x)+o⁡(1){x}^{-\varrho}h\bigl(\lfloor x\rfloor\bigr)=P\bigl(\log_{2}{x}\bigr)+o(1). Similarly, x−ϱ​h​(⌈x⌉)=P⁡(log2⁡x)+o⁡(1){x}^{-\varrho}h\bigl(\lceil x\rceil\bigr)=P\bigl(\log_{2}{x}\bigr)+o(1), and (ii) follows. ∎

Proposition 2.12.

Suppose that g⁡(x)g(x) is a continuous function on (0,∞)(0,\infty) with g⁡(x)=0g(x)=0 for x⩽1x\leqslant 1. Define

h⁡(x):=∑k⩾02k​ϱ​g​(2−k​x).h(x):=\sum_{k\geqslant 0}2^{k\varrho}g(2^{-k}x). (2.32)

Then, the following are equivalent.

  1. (i)

    x−ϱ​h​(x)=P1​(log2⁡x)+o⁡(1)x^{-\varrho}h(x)=P_{1}(\log_{2}x)+o(1) as x→∞x\to\infty, for some continuous 11-periodic function P1P_{1} on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

  2. (ii)

    x−ϱ​h​(x)=P1​(log2⁡x)+o⁡(1)x^{-\varrho}h(x)=P_{1}(\log_{2}x)+o(1) as x→∞x\to\infty, for some 11-periodic function P1P_{1} on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

  3. (iii)

    Q⁡(x):=∑k⩾12−ϱ​k​g​(2k​x)Q(x):=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}2^{-\varrho k}g(2^{k}x) converges uniformly for x∈[1,2]x\in[1,2].

Furthermore, when these conditions hold, Q⁡(x)Q(x) is defined for all x>0x>0, Q⁡(x)=o⁡(xϱ)Q(x)=o(x^{\varrho}) as x→∞x\to\infty,

P1​(t)=∑m∈ℤ2−ϱ⁡(m+t)​g​(2m+t),t∈ℝ,P_{1}(t)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}2^{-\varrho(m+t)}g(2^{m+t}),\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}, (2.33)

and

h⁡(x)=xϱ​P1​(log2⁡x)−Q⁡(x),x>0.h(x)=x^{\varrho}P_{1}(\log_{2}x)-Q(x),\qquad x>0. (2.34)
Proof.

Again, the proof differs mainly notationally from the proofs of the corresponding implications in [27, Theorem 2], and we omit some details. Let Gm​(x):=∑k=0m2−ϱ​k​g​(2k​x)G_{m}(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{m}2^{-\varrho k}g(2^{k}x), and note that (iii) is equivalent to the property that Gm​(x)G_{m}(x) converges uniformly on [1,2][1,2] to G⁡(x):=Q⁡(x)+g⁡(x)G(x):=Q(x)+g(x).

(i)⟹\implies(ii). Trivial.

(ii)⟹\implies(iii). Suppose that y∈[1,2]y\in[1,2] and m⩾0m\geqslant 0. Then (2.32) yields

h⁡(2m​y)=∑0⩽k⩽m2k​ϱ​g​(2−k+m​y)=∑0⩽j⩽m2(m−j)​ϱ​g​(2j​y)=2m​ϱ​Gm​(y).\displaystyle h\bigl(2^{m}y\bigr)=\sum_{0\leqslant k\leqslant m}2^{k\varrho}g\bigl(2^{-k+m}y\bigr)=\sum_{0\leqslant j\leqslant m}2^{(m-j)\varrho}g\bigl(2^{j}y\bigr)=2^{m\varrho}G_{m}(y). (2.35)

Hence, taking x=2m​yx=2^{m}y, (ii) implies, as m→∞m\to\infty, uniformly for y∈[1,2]y\in[1,2],

y−ϱ​Gm​(y)=(2m​y)−ϱ​h​(2m​y)=P1​(m+log2⁡y)+o⁡(1)=P1​(log2⁡y)+o⁡(1).\displaystyle y^{-\varrho}G_{m}(y)=(2^{m}y)^{-\varrho}h\bigl(2^{m}y\bigr)=P_{1}\bigl(m+\log_{2}y\bigr)+o(1)=P_{1}\bigl(\log_{2}y\bigr)+o(1). (2.36)

Hence y−ϱ​Gm​(y)y^{-\varrho}G_{m}(y) converges uniformly on [1,2][1,2], and thus Gm​(y)G_{m}(y) converges uniformly on [1,2][1,2].

(iii)⟹\implies(i). Conversely, (2.35) now yields

(2m​y)−ϱ​h​(2m​y)=y−ϱ​Gm​(y)=y−ϱ​G​(y)+o⁡(1)\displaystyle(2^{m}y)^{-\varrho}h\bigl(2^{m}y\bigr)=y^{-\varrho}G_{m}(y)=y^{-\varrho}G(y)+o(1) (2.37)

as m→∞m\to\infty, uniformly for y∈[1,2]y\in[1,2]. Next, we show that

P1​(t):=∑m∈ℤ2−ϱ⁡(m+t)​g​(2m+t).\displaystyle P_{1}(t):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}2^{-\varrho(m+t)}g\bigl(2^{m+t}\bigr). (2.38)

is a well-defined 11-periodic function. First, if t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], then all terms with m<0m<0 vanish and thus

P1​(t):=∑m⩾02−ϱ⁡(m+t)​g​(2m+t)=2−ϱ​t​G​(2t),\displaystyle P_{1}(t):=\sum_{m\geqslant 0}2^{-\varrho(m+t)}g\bigl(2^{m+t}\bigr)=2^{-\varrho t}G(2^{t}), (2.39)

where the sum converges uniformly for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] by assumption. This shows that the sum in (2.38) converges for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], and that P1​(t)P_{1}(t) is continuous there. Furthermore, the sum in (2.38) is 11-periodic in tt, and thus the sum converges for all real tt and defines a 11-periodic continuous function P1​(t)P_{1}(t).

Taking m=Lxm=L_{x} and y=2θxy=2^{\theta_{x}} in (2.37) yields as x→∞x\to\infty, using (2.39) and the periodicity of P1P_{1},

x−ϱ​h​(x)=2−ϱ​θx​G​(2θx)+o⁡(1)=P1​(θx)+o⁡(1)=P1​(log2⁡x)+o⁡(1).\displaystyle x^{-\varrho}h(x)=2^{-\varrho\theta_{x}}G\bigl(2^{\theta_{x}}\bigr)+o(1)=P_{1}\bigl(\theta_{x}\bigr)+o(1)=P_{1}\bigl(\log_{2}x\bigr)+o(1). (2.40)

Hence (i) holds.

Finally, (2.33) is (2.38), which also shows that the sum defining Q⁡(x)Q(x) converges for all x>0x>0, and that

h⁡(x)+Q⁡(x)\displaystyle h(x)+Q(x) =∑k⩾02k​ϱ​g​(2−k​x)+∑k⩾12−ϱ​k​g​(2k​x)\displaystyle=\sum_{k\geqslant 0}2^{k\varrho}g(2^{-k}x)+\sum_{k\geqslant 1}2^{-\varrho k}g(2^{k}x)
=∑k∈ℤ2−k​ϱ​g​(2k​x)\displaystyle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}2^{-k\varrho}g(2^{k}x)
=xϱ​P1​(log2⁡x).\displaystyle=x^{\varrho}P_{1}\bigl(\log_{2}x\bigr). (2.41)

Moreover,

(2m​x)−ϱ​Q​(2m​x)=x−ϱ​∑k⩾12−ϱ⁡(k+m)​g​(2k+m​x)=x−ϱ​∑k⩾m+12−ϱ​k​g​(2k​x),\displaystyle(2^{m}x)^{-\varrho}Q(2^{m}x)=x^{-\varrho}\sum_{k\geqslant 1}2^{-\varrho(k+m)}g(2^{k+m}x)=x^{-\varrho}\sum_{k\geqslant m+1}2^{-\varrho k}g(2^{k}x), (2.42)

which by (iii) converges to 0 as m→∞m\to\infty, uniformly for x∈[1,2]x\in[1,2]. Hence, x−ϱ​Q​(x)→0x^{-\varrho}Q(x)\to 0 as x→∞x\to\infty.

This completes the proof of the proposition. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.10.

First, (i)⇔\iff(ii) follows from Proposition 2.11, with h⁡(x)=f⁡(x)h(x)=f(x).

Next, define h⁡(x):=f⁡(x)−xϱ​f​(1)​P0​(log2⁡x)h(x):=f(x)-x^{\varrho}f(1)P_{0}\bigl(\log_{2}x\bigr), and note that (2.21) implies (2.32). Thus (ii)⇔\iff(iii)⇔\iff(iv) and the last sentence of the statement follow from Proposition 2.12, with P⁡(t):=f⁡(1)​P0​(t)+P1​(t)P(t):=f(1)P_{0}(t)+P_{1}(t). ∎

A more practical condition than uniform convergence is the following.

Corollary 2.13.

Define

Am:=sup2m⩽n⩽2m+1|g⁡(n)|.A_{m}:=\sup_{2^{m}\leqslant n\leqslant 2^{m+1}}|g(n)|. (2.43)

If ∑m2−m​ϱ​Am<∞\,\sum_{m}2^{-m\varrho}A_{m}<\infty then (2.27) and (2.29) hold, where PP is continuous, periodic and given by (2.30). ∎

Corollary 2.14.

Suppose that g⁡(n)=O⁡(nϱ−ε)g(n)=O\bigl(n^{\varrho-\varepsilon}\bigr) for some ε>0\varepsilon>0. Then (2.27) and (2.29) hold with PP continuous, periodic and given by (2.30), and Q⁡(x)=O⁡(xϱ−ε)Q(x)=O(x^{\varrho-\varepsilon}). ∎

Example 2.15.

One simple but important case is when g⁡(n)=0g(n)=0, n⩾2n\geqslant 2, i.e., the recurrence Λα,β​[f]=0\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f]=0. By suitable normalisations, we may assume f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1. As the sequence ff satisfying Λα,β​[f]=0\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f]=0 with f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1 plays a fundamental role in most of our applications, we denote the solution by Sα,β​(n)S_{\alpha,\beta}(n) throughout this paper.

Theorem 2.10 applies trivially, with Q⁡(x)=0Q(x)=0 and P​(t)=P0​(t)P(t)=P_{0}(t), and thus

Sα,β​(n)=f⁡(n)=nlog2⁡(α+β)​P0​(log2⁡n),n⩾1,\displaystyle S_{\alpha,\beta}(n)=f(n)=n^{\log_{2}(\alpha+\beta)}P_{0}(\log_{2}n),\qquad n\geqslant 1, (2.44)

where P0​(t)P_{0}(t) is given by (2.22); thus also, more explicitly,

Sα,β​(n)\displaystyle S_{\alpha,\beta}(n) =(1+(α+β−1)​φ​(2{log2⁡n}−1))​(α+β)⌊log2⁡n⌋.\displaystyle=\bigl(1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi\bigl({2^{\{\log_{2}n\}}-1}\bigr)\bigr)(\alpha+\beta)^{\lfloor\log_{2}n\rfloor}. (2.45)

(In the case α=β\alpha=\beta, when φ⁡(x)=x\varphi(x)=x by Remark 2.4, (2.44) was found, in an equivalent form, by [14].) ∎

Example 2.16.

Another simple but important case is when g⁡(2​m)=0g(2m)=0 for all m⩾1m\geqslant 1, i.e., g⁡(n)g(n) is non-zero only for odd nn. Suppose also, for example, that g⁡(n)=O⁡(nϱ−ε)g(n)=O(n^{\varrho-\varepsilon}) so that Corollary 2.14 applies. Then, (2.28) shows that Q⁡(n)=0Q(n)=0 for every integer nn, and thus (2.29) yields the identity f⁡(n)=nϱ​P​(log2⁡n)f(n)=n^{\varrho}P(\log_{2}n), n⩾1n\geqslant 1. ∎

Remark 2.17.

We have here studied the case with oo-estimates and convergence in e.g. Theorem 2.10. Analogously, we note that it follows easily from Lemma 2.7 and (2.35) that

f⁡(n)=O⁡(nϱ)⇔f⁡(x)=O⁡(xϱ)for ​x⩾1⇔∑0⩽k⩽m2−ϱ​kg(2kx)=O(1)for x∈[1,2] and m⩾0.\begin{split}f(n)=O(n^{\varrho})&\iff f(x)=O(x^{\varrho})\quad\text{for }x\geqslant 1\\ &\iff\sum_{0\leqslant k\leqslant m}2^{-\varrho k}g(2^{k}x)=O(1)\quad\text{for $x\in[1,2]$ and $m\geqslant 0$}.\end{split} (2.46)

∎

Remark 2.18.

We concentrate in this paper on the case when g⁡(n)g(n) grows more slowly than nϱn^{\varrho} (and (2.28) converges), and thus the sums in (2.20) and (2.21) are dominated by terms with kk large (more precisely, k=Lx+O⁡(1)k=L_{x}+O(1) in (2.21)). One might also consider the opposite case, when g⁡(n)g(n) grows more rapidly that nϱn^{\varrho}. In this case, the sums in (2.20) and (2.21) are dominated by their first terms, which shows that (typically, at least) f⁡(n)f(n) grows at the same rate as g⁡(n)g(n), and has the same smoothness properties. (In particular, there is no smoothening effect as we can see in (2.29).) We consider one example as part of Example 5.10, but we otherwise leave this case to a future study. (Except for several examples where we reduce to a slower growing gg by subtracting a polynomial.) ∎

3 Smoothness properties of the periodic function PP

We prove in this section that under certain conditions on g⁡(n)g(n) stronger than those in Theorem 2.10, the periodic function PP is Hölder continuous, and has an absolutely convergent Fourier series expansion. We also show that the interpolating function φ\varphi is Hölder continuous, and thus the interpolated function f⁡(x)f(x) is not only continuous but always locally Hölder continuous.

In this section, starting from the recursion (1.1), we tacitly assume that α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0 and g⁡(1)=0g(1)=0; also P0P_{0}, P1P_{1} and PP are functions defined as in Section 2; furthermore, we define

λ:=log2⁡α+βα∨β∈(0,1].\displaystyle\lambda:=\log_{2}\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\vee\beta}\in(0,1]. (3.1)

Note that λ=1\lambda=1 if and only if α=β\alpha=\beta.

Bounded variation, Lipschitz continuity and Hölder continuity.

We recall some standard definitions. A function ϕ\phi is Lipschitz continuous on an interval [a,b][a,b] if there exists a positive number CC such that

|ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(y)|⩽C​|x−y|(​x,y∈[a,b]​).|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|\leqslant C|x-y|\quad\text{(}x,y\in[a,b]\text{).} (3.2)

This definition extends to Hölder continuity by replacing the last inequality by

|ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(y)|⩽C​|x−y|γ(​x,y∈[a,b]​),|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|\leqslant C|x-y|^{\gamma}\quad\text{(}x,y\in[a,b]\text{)}, (3.3)

for some 0<γ⩽10<\gamma\leqslant 1. Let Hγ​[a,b]\mathrm{H}_{\gamma}[a,b] be the space of functions ϕ\phi on [a,b][a,b] such that the seminorm

‖ϕ‖Hγ​[a,b]′:=supa⩽x<y⩽b|ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(y)||x−y|γ\|\phi\|^{\prime}_{\mathrm{H}_{\gamma}[a,b]}:=\sup_{a\leqslant x<y\leqslant b}\frac{|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|}{|x-y|^{\gamma}} (3.4)

is finite; this is a Banach space with the norm

‖ϕ‖Hγ​[a,b]:=‖ϕ‖Hγ​[a,b]′+supx∈[a,b]|ϕ⁡(x)|.\|\phi\|_{\mathrm{H}_{\gamma}[a,b]}:=\|\phi\|^{\prime}_{\mathrm{H}_{\gamma}[a,b]}+\sup_{x\in[a,b]}|\phi(x)|. (3.5)

A function ϕ\phi is of bounded variation on [a,b][a,b] if its total variation is bounded. Such a function is differentiable almost everywhere. Let BV⁡[a,b]\mathrm{BV}[a,b] be the space of functions on [a,b][a,b] of bounded variation, with the norm

‖ϕ‖BV⁡[a,b]:=V⁡(ϕ,a,b)+sup[a,b]|ϕ|,\|\phi\|_{\mathrm{BV}[a,b]}:=V(\phi;a,b)+\sup_{[a,b]}|\phi|, (3.6)

where VV denotes the total variation.

Note that both BV⁡[a,b]\mathrm{BV}[a,b] and Hγ​[a,b]\mathrm{H}_{\gamma}[a,b] are Banach algebras. Also H1⊂BV\mathrm{H}_{1}\subset\mathrm{BV}, namely, Lipschitz continuity implies bounded variation.

Smoothness of φ\varphi and PP.

We prove first that the interpolating function φ\varphi is Hölder continuous. Note that φ\varphi is trivially of bounded variation since it is monotone.

Lemma 3.1.

φ∈Hλ​[0,1]\varphi\in\mathrm{H}_{\lambda}[0,1].

Proof.

First, let x=m​2−Nx=m2^{-N} and y=(m+1)​2−Ny=(m+1)2^{-N} for some integers N⩾0N\geqslant 0 and m<2Nm<2^{N}. Then (2.14) implies

φ⁡(y)−φ⁡(x)⩽(α∨βα+β)N=(2−λ)N=2−N​λ.\displaystyle\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)\leqslant\Bigl(\frac{\alpha\vee\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\Bigr)^{N}=\bigl(2^{-\lambda}\bigr)^{N}=2^{-N\lambda}. (3.7)

For general xx and yy with 0⩽x<y⩽10\leqslant x<y\leqslant 1, let N:=⌈−log2⁡(y−x)⌉N:=\lceil-\log_{2}\left(y-x\right)\rceil and k:=⌊x​2N⌋k:=\lfloor x2^{N}\rfloor. Then 2−N⩽y−x⩽21−N2^{-N}\leqslant y-x\leqslant 2^{1-N} and k​2−N⩽x<y⩽(k+3)​2−Nk2^{-N}\leqslant x<y\leqslant(k+3)2^{-N}. Hence, using (3.7) thrice,

φ⁡(y)−φ⁡(x)⩽φ⁡((k+3)​2−N)−φ⁡(k​2−N)⩽3⋅2−N​λ⩽3​|y−x|λ.\varphi(y)-\varphi(x)\leqslant\varphi\bigl((k+3)2^{-N}\bigr)-\varphi\bigl(k2^{-N}\bigr)\leqslant 3\cdot 2^{-N\lambda}\leqslant 3|y-x|^{\lambda}. (3.8)

This proves that φ∈Hλ​[0,1]\varphi\in\mathrm{H}_{\lambda}[0,1]. ∎

Lemma 3.2.

P0∈Hλ​[0,1]∩BV⁡[0,1]P_{0}\in\mathrm{H}_{\lambda}[0,1]\cap\mathrm{BV}[0,1].

Proof.

For t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], we may replace {t}\{t\} by tt in (2.22). It then follows from Lemma 3.1 that the first factor in (2.22) belongs to Hλ​[0,1]\mathrm{H}_{\lambda}[0,1], and so does the second factor since it has a bounded derivative. Hence, P0∈Hλ​[0,1]P_{0}\in\mathrm{H}_{\lambda}[0,1].

Similarly, both factors in (2.22) then are monotone on [0,1)[0,1), and therefore of bounded variation. Hence P0∈BV⁡[0,1]P_{0}\in\mathrm{BV}[0,1]. ∎

To treat the function PP, we need a smoothness assumption on the sequence g⁡(n)g(n). Let

Am:=max2m⩽n⩽2m+1⁡|g⁡(n)|andBm:=max2m⩽n<2m+1⁡|g⁡(n+1)−g⁡(n)|.\displaystyle A_{m}:=\max_{2^{m}\leqslant n\leqslant 2^{m+1}}|g(n)|\quad\text{and}\quad B_{m}:=\max_{2^{m}\leqslant n<2^{m+1}}|g(n+1)-g(n)|. (3.9)
Lemma 3.3.

If ϱ>0\varrho>0 and

∑m⩾02(1−ϱ)​m​Bm<∞,\sum_{m\geqslant 0}2^{(1-\varrho)m}B_{m}<\infty, (3.10)

then

∑m⩾02−ϱ​m​Am<∞.\displaystyle\sum_{m\geqslant 0}2^{-\varrho m}A_{m}<\infty. (3.11)

Note that ϱ>0\varrho>0 is equivalent to α+β>1\alpha+\beta>1.

Proof.

Let m⩾1m\geqslant 1. For every nn lying in the interval 2m⩽n⩽2m+12^{m}\leqslant n\leqslant 2^{m+1},

|g⁡(n)|\displaystyle|g(n)| ⩽|g⁡(2)|+∑2⩽j<n|g⁡(j+1)−g⁡(j)|\displaystyle\leqslant|g(2)|+\sum_{2\leqslant j<n}|g(j+1)-g(j)|
⩽|g⁡(2)|+∑1⩽k⩽m2k​Bk,\displaystyle\leqslant|g(2)|+\sum_{1\leqslant k\leqslant m}2^{k}B_{k}, (3.12)

implying that

Am⩽|g⁡(2)|+∑1⩽k⩽m2k​Bk.A_{m}\leqslant|g(2)|+\sum_{1\leqslant k\leqslant m}2^{k}B_{k}. (3.13)

Thus,

=|g⁡(2)|​2−ϱ1−2−ϱ+11−2−ϱ​∑k⩾12(1−ϱ)​k​Bk.\displaystyle=|g(2)|\frac{2^{-\varrho}}{1-2^{-\varrho}}+\frac{1}{1-2^{-\varrho}}\sum_{k\geqslant 1}2^{(1-\varrho)k}B_{k}. (3.14)

This proves the lemma. ∎

Lemma 3.4.

If ϱ>0\varrho>0 and (3.10) holds, then P∈Hλ​[0,1]∩BV⁡[0,1]P\in\mathrm{H}_{\lambda}[0,1]\cap\mathrm{BV}[0,1].

where, furthermore, by the definitions (3.4)–(3.5) and (3.9),

Remark 3.5.

Lemma 3.1 is best possible: φ∉Hγ​[0,1]\varphi\notin\mathrm{H}_{\gamma}[0,1] for γ>λ\gamma>\lambda. In particular, φ\varphi is not Lipschitz continuous (and not differentiable) unless α=β\alpha=\beta. To see this, it suffices to note that (2.14) yields φ⁡(2−j)−φ⁡(0)=(βα+β)j\varphi(2^{-j})-\varphi(0)=\bigl(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\bigr)^{j} and φ⁡(1)−φ⁡(1−2−j)=(αα+β)j\varphi(1)-\varphi(1-2^{-j})=\bigl(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\bigr)^{j} for all j⩾1j\geqslant 1, and one of these equals (α∨βα+β)j=(2−j)λ\bigl(\frac{\alpha\vee\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\bigr)^{j}=\bigl(2^{-j}\bigr)^{\lambda}.

Hence, (2.22) shows that if α+β≠1\alpha+\beta\neq 1, then also Lemma 3.2 is best possible: P0∉Hγ​[0,1]P_{0}\notin\mathrm{H}_{\gamma}[0,1] for γ>λ\gamma>\lambda. Furthermore, (2.30) shows that typically also P∉Hγ​[0,1]P\notin\mathrm{H}_{\gamma}[0,1] for γ>λ\gamma>\lambda. (Also in the case f⁡(1)=0f(1)=0, since g⁡(x)g(x) has the same smoothness as φ\varphi.) However, note that PP may be more smooth in special cases (which means that there is cancellation of non-smoothness in (2.30)); for example, we may take any continuously differentiable periodic function P⁡(t)P(t) and let f⁡(n):=nϱ​P​(log2⁡n)f(n):=n^{\varrho}P(\log_{2}n) and then define g⁡(n)g(n) by (2.1).

Fourier series.

The periodic function P⁡(t)P(t) may be described by its Fourier coefficients; these are given by the following formula, where we use the notation

χk:=2​k​πlog⁡2​i,k∈ℤ.\displaystyle\chi_{k}:=\frac{2k\pi}{\log 2}i,\qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}. (3.24)
Theorem 3.6.

(i)  If Theorem 2.10(iv) holds (and thus all statements in Theorem 2.10), then the Fourier coefficients P^​(k):=∫01P⁡(t)​e−2​k​π​i​t​𝑑t\widehat{P}(k):=\int_{0}^{1}P(t)e^{-2k\pi it}\,\mathrm{d}t of P⁡(t)P(t) are given by

P^​(k)=1log⁡2​∫1∞g⁡(u)uϱ+χk+1​𝑑u+f⁡(1)log⁡2​∫011+(α+β−1)​φ​(u)(1+u)ϱ+χk+1​𝑑u,\widehat{P}(k)=\frac{1}{\log 2}\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{g(u)}{u^{\varrho+\chi_{k}+1}}\,\mathrm{d}u+\frac{f(1)}{\log 2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi(u)}{(1+u)^{\varrho+\chi_{k}+1}}\,\mathrm{d}u, (3.25)

where the first integral is (at least) conditionally convergent.

(ii)  If (3.11) holds, then (3.25) holds, with absolutely convergent integrals.

(iii)  If α+β>1\alpha+\beta>1 and (3.10) holds, then P⁡(t)P(t) has an absolutely convergent Fourier series P⁡(t)=∑k∈ℤP^​(k)​e2​π​i​k​tP(t)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\widehat{P}(k)e^{2\pi ikt}, for t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, where the coefficients are given by (3.25), with absolutely convergent integrals.

Proof.

3.6: The Fourier coefficients of P⁡(t)P(t) are given by, using the definitions (2.30), (1.3) and (2.22),

P^​(k)\displaystyle\widehat{P}(k) :=∫01P⁡(t)​e−2​k​π​i​t​𝑑t\displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{1}P(t)e^{-2k\pi it}\,\mathrm{d}t
=∑m∈ℤ∫01g⁡(2m+t)​2−ϱ⁡(m+t)​e−2​k​π​i​t​𝑑t\displaystyle=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}\int_{0}^{1}g\left(2^{m+t}\right)2^{-\varrho(m+t)}e^{-2k\pi it}\,\mathrm{d}t
+f(1)∫01(1+(α+β−1)φ(2t−1))(α+β)−te−2​k​π​i​tdt\displaystyle\qquad+f(1)\int_{0}^{1}\left(1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi\left(2^{t}-1\right)\right)(\alpha+\beta)^{-t}e^{-2k\pi it}\,\mathrm{d}t
=∫−∞∞g⁡(2t)​2−ϱ​t​e−2​k​π​i​t​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(2^{t})2^{-\varrho t}e^{-2k\pi it}\,\mathrm{d}t
+f(1)∫01(1+(α+β−1)φ(2t−1))2−ϱ​te−2​k​π​i​tdt,\displaystyle\qquad+f(1)\int_{0}^{1}\left(1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi\left(2^{t}-1\right)\right)2^{-\varrho t}e^{-2k\pi it}\,\mathrm{d}t, (3.26)

where the sum and the integral over (−∞,∞)(-\infty,\infty) are (conditionally) convergent because the sum in (2.30) converges uniformly, and g⁡(x)=0g(x)=0 for x⩽1x\leqslant 1. (The integrals over [0,1][0,1] are, trivially, absolutely convergent.) Finally, (3.25) follows by the changes of variables u=2tu=2^{t} and u=2t−1u=2^{t}-1, respectively, in the two integrals.

3.6: Corollary 2.13 shows that all statements in Theorem 3.6 hold, and thus part 3.6 applies, which gives (3.25). The absolute convergence of the first integral follows by (3.11).

3.6: By Lemma 3.3, we have (3.11), and thus 3.6 applies. Since PP is a continuous 11-periodic function, the absolute convergence of the Fourier series follows directly from Lemma 3.4 by a theorem of Zygmund (see [43, p. 241, VI.(3.6)] or [30, p. 35]). ∎

The formula (3.25) shows a connection with Mellin transforms; this is explored further in Appendix A.

The conditions of Theorem 3.63.6 are, of course, not necessary for absolute convergence of the Fourier series of P⁡(t)P(t). Another simple case is the following.

Example 3.7.

If α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0 and g⁡(n)=0g(n)=0, n⩾2n\geqslant 2, we may normalise by f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1 as in Example 2.15; thus f​(n)=Sα,β​(n)f(n)=S_{\alpha,\beta}(n) and (2.44) holds. In the case α=β\alpha=\beta, the integrals in (3.25) can easily be evaluated explicitly, and we obtain the following extension of the case α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1 in [27, Theorem 3]. Let, as in [27],

If α=β>0\alpha=\beta>0 and Theorem 2.10(iv) holds (and thus all statements in Theorem 2.10), then, assuming ϱ+χk≠0,1\varrho+\chi_{k}\neq 0,1,

P^​(k)\displaystyle\widehat{P}(k) =1(ϱ+χk)​(ϱ−1+χk)​log⁡2​(D⁡(ϱ−1+χk)+(2​α−1)​(α−1)α​f​(1)).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(\varrho+\chi_{k})(\varrho-1+\chi_{k})\log 2}\Bigl(D(\varrho-1+\chi_{k})+\frac{(2\alpha-1)(\alpha-1)}{\alpha}f(1)\Bigr). (3.29)

The two exceptional cases are k=0k=0 and either α=β=12\alpha=\beta=\frac{1}{2} or α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1; in these cases, (3.29) is of the form 0/00/0 and is replaced by a suitable limit form. Proof.

∫1∞g⁡(u)uϱ+χk+1​𝑑u=D⁡(ϱ−1+χk)(ϱ+χk)​(ϱ−1+χk),\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{g(u)}{u^{\varrho+\chi_{k}+1}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\frac{D(\varrho-1+\chi_{k})}{(\varrho+\chi_{k})(\varrho-1+\chi_{k})}, (3.30)

with the sum (3.27) converging at least conditionally.

∫011+(2​α−1)​u(1+u)ϱ+χk+1​𝑑u\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1+(2\alpha-1)u}{(1+u)^{\varrho+\chi_{k}+1}}\,\mathrm{d}u =∫01(2​α−1(1+u)ϱ+χk+2−2​α(1+u)ϱ+χk+1)​𝑑u\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{2\alpha-1}{(1+u)^{\varrho+\chi_{k}}}+\frac{2-2\alpha}{(1+u)^{\varrho+\chi_{k}+1}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u
=(2​α−1)​(α−1)α⋅1(ϱ+χk)​(ϱ−1+χk).\displaystyle=\frac{(2\alpha-1)(\alpha-1)}{\alpha}\cdot\frac{1}{(\varrho+\chi_{k})(\varrho-1+\chi_{k})}. (3.31)

Using (3.30)–(3.31) in (3.25) yields (3.29). ∎

For later use we note that, still assuming α=β\alpha=\beta, if the condition Theorem 2.10(iv) holds, then [27, (2.23)] more generally yields the Mellin transform

∫1∞g⁡(u)us+1​𝑑u=D⁡(s−1)s⁡(s−1)\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{g(u)}{u^{s+1}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\frac{D(s-1)}{s(s-1)} (3.32)

Let α=β>0\alpha=\beta>0, and consider P0​(t)P_{0}(t) given by (2.25) in Remark 2.8. By Corollary 3.8, with g⁡(n)=0g(n)=0 and f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1 (and thus D⁡(s)=0D(s)=0), we have the Fourier coefficients, assuming ϱ+χk≠0,1\varrho+\chi_{k}\neq 0,1:

4 Applications, I. α≠β\alpha\neq\beta

We discuss applications of our results in this section, grouping them according to the growth order of gg. Most examples are taken from OEIS, sometimes with a shift of the index (which for simplicity of presentation is not explicitly specified in this paper). For example, if

f⁡(n)=α​f​(⌊n+d2⌋)+β​f​(⌈n+d2⌉)+g⁡(n)(n⩾n0⩾1),\displaystyle f(n)=\alpha f\bigl({\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{n+d}{2}\bigr\rfloor}\bigr)+\beta f\bigl({\bigl\lceil\tfrac{n+d}{2}\bigr\rceil}\bigr)+g(n)\qquad(n\geqslant n_{0}\geqslant 1), (4.1)

then f¯​(n):=f​(n+d)\bar{f}(n):=f(n+d) satisfies

f¯​(n)=α​f¯​(⌊n2⌋)+β​f¯​(⌈n2⌉)+g⁡(n+d)(n⩾n0−d).\displaystyle\bar{f}(n)=\alpha\bar{f}\bigl({\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\bigr\rfloor}\bigr)+\beta\bar{f}\bigl({\bigl\lceil\tfrac{n}{2}\bigr\rceil}\bigr)+g(n+d)\qquad(n\geqslant n_{0}-d). (4.2)

Note also that if (1.1) holds only for n⩾n0n\geqslant n_{0}, we can make it hold for all n⩾2n\geqslant 2 by redefining g⁡(n)g(n) for 2⩽n<n02\leqslant n<n_{0}. See A294456 (contained in Example 5.3) for an example.

Some of the examples are defined in OEIS by a recursion of the form (1.1); in other examples, such a recursion is stated as a property; in yet other examples below, no such recursion is given explicitly in OEIS, but can be concluded from other properties given there. Of course, every sequence f⁡(n)f(n) satisfies Λα,β​[f]=g\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f]=g for some sequence g⁡(n)g(n); we are only interested in cases when g⁡(n)g(n) has a simple explicit form, and in particular does not grow too fast. We regard polynomial terms in f⁡(n)f(n) as essentially trivial, so we also include examples when they dominate ff and the periodic fluctuations constitute a lower-order term. (In such cases our theorems apply only after subtracting a suitable polynomial.)

To avoid trivialities, we discard in our discussions sequences from OEIS whose generating functions are rational with all singularities on the unit circle. (For example, polynomials.) Such sequences are in the thousands in OEIS.

For notational convenience, we insert the subscript to φ\varphi by writing φα,β​(t)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(t) whenever necessary. The symbols f⁡(n),g⁡(n)f(n),g(n) and P⁡(t)P(t) are all generic and may differ from one instance to the other; we also specify explicitly them as fA006046​(n)f_{\text{A006046}}(n), gA006046​(n)g_{\text{A006046}}(n), and PA006046​(t)P_{\text{A006046}}(t) if needed. Note that our indexing of the sequence ff may differ from that on OEIS by a shift; for example, fA006581​(n)=A006581​(n+1)f_{\text{A006581}}(n)=\text{A006581}(n+1) for n⩾1n\geqslant 1. Also the format g⁡(n)={⋯⋯g(n)=\begin{cases}\cdots\\ \cdots\end{cases} in the tables without explicit mention always means the values of g⁡(n)g(n) in the even and odd cases, respectively.

We continue to assume α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, and consider in this section cases with α≠β\alpha\neq\beta. On the other hand, examples in the special cases when α=β\alpha=\beta exhibit more structural properties and explicit expressions, and will be discussed in Section 5. The properties are very similar to the case when α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1 that we already examined in detail in [27], although there are also subtle differences on the smoothness of the periodic functions.

4.1 Periodic equivalence

We introduce a simple notion here, very useful in identifying the relation between sequences. The main case is when two sequences f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} both satisfy Theorem 2.10 (with the same ϱ\varrho), and the corresponding periodic functions P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} are the same, or more generally proportional. It will be convenient to be a bit more general, and regard polynomial terms as trivial. We thus define:

Definition 4.1.

Two sequences f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} are said to be periodically equivalent if, for some ϱ\varrho, fj​(n)=nϱ​Pj​(log2⁡n)+pj​(n)f_{j}(n)=n^{\varrho}P_{j}(\log_{2}n)+p_{j}(n), j=1,2j=1,2, where pj​(n)p_{j}(n) are polynomials and PjP_{j} are periodic functions such that P1​(k)=c​P2​(k){P}_{1}(k)=c{P}_{2}(k) for some constant c≠0c\neq 0. For simplicity, we write f1≎f2f_{1}\Bumpeq f_{2}.

It is possible to extend the definition to asymptotically periodic equivalence by allowing fj​(n)=nϱ​Pj​(log2⁡n)+pj​(n)+o⁡(nϱ)f_{j}(n)=n^{\varrho}P_{j}(\log_{2}n)+p_{j}(n)+o(n^{\varrho}) for j=1,2j=1,2, but the above definition without o⁡(1)o(1)-term is sufficient for our use in this paper.

We begin with the simplest cases when Λα,β​[f]​(n)=g⁡(n)=0\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f](n)=g(n)=0. Such cases cover also the situation when g⁡(n)=cg(n)=c for n⩾2n\geqslant 2 because normalising ff by f¯​(n):=f​(n)+cα+β−1\bar{f}(n):=f(n)+\frac{c}{\alpha+\beta-1} yields the recurrence Λα,β​[f¯]=0\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[\bar{f}]=0 with f¯​(1)=f​(1)+cα+β−1\bar{f}(1)=f(1)+\frac{c}{\alpha+\beta-1}. For convenience of reference, we state this observation, in a somewhat generalised form, as a lemma.

Lemma 4.2.

If α+β>1\alpha+\beta>1, then two sequences defined by Λα,β​[f1]=0\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f_{1}]=0 with f1​(1)≠0f_{1}(1)\neq 0 and Λα,β​[f2]=c\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f_{2}]=c are connected by

f2​(n)=(f2​(1)+cα+β−1)​f1​(n)f1​(1)−cα+β−1.\displaystyle f_{2}(n)=\left(f_{2}(1)+\frac{c}{\alpha+\beta-1}\right)\frac{f_{1}(n)}{f_{1}(1)}-\frac{c}{\alpha+\beta-1}. (4.3)

Hence, if f2​(1)+cα+β−1≠0f_{2}(1)+\frac{c}{\alpha+\beta-1}\neq 0, the sequences f1​(n)f_{1}(n) and f2​(n)f_{2}(n) are periodically equivalent with the underlying periodic function PP satisfying P∈Hλ​[0,1]∩BV⁡[0,1]P\in\mathrm{H}_{\lambda}[0,1]\cap\mathrm{BV}[0,1], where λ\lambda is defined in (3.1).

Proof.

It is easy to verify that (4.3) satisfies the recursion Λα,β​[f2]=c\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f_{2}]=c. and thus (4.3) holds by induction. Thus f1≎f2f_{1}\Bumpeq f_{2} if f2​(1)+cα+β−1≠0f_{2}(1)+\frac{c}{\alpha+\beta-1}\neq 0. The Hölder continuity and bounded variation of PP follow from Lemma 3.4. ∎

Lemma 4.3.

Write f∼Λ^α,β​[c;d,e]f\sim\widehat{\Lambda}_{\alpha,\beta}[c;d,e] if Λα,β​[f]=c​n+{d,n evene,n odd\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f]=cn+\begin{cases}d,&\text{$n$ even}\\ e,&\text{$n$ odd}\end{cases} for n⩾2n\geqslant 2. Suppose that α+β>2\alpha+\beta>2, and that

f1∼Λ^α,β​[c;d,e]andf2∼Λ^α,β​[0;0,(α−β)​cα+β−2−d+e],\displaystyle f_{1}\sim\widehat{\Lambda}_{\alpha,\beta}[c;d,e]\quad\text{and}\quad f_{2}\sim\widehat{\Lambda}_{\alpha,\beta}\left[0;0,\frac{(\alpha-\beta)c}{\alpha+\beta-2}-d+e\right], (4.4)

where f2​(1)=f1​(1)+2​cα+β−2+dα+β−1≠0f_{2}(1)=f_{1}(1)+\frac{2c}{\alpha+\beta-2}+\frac{d}{\alpha+\beta-1}\neq 0. Then f1≎f2f_{1}\Bumpeq f_{2}. Furthermore,

f1​(n)=nϱ​P​(log2⁡n)−2​c​nα+β−2−dα+β−1(n⩾1)\displaystyle f_{1}(n)=n^{\varrho}P(\log_{2}n)-\frac{2cn}{\alpha+\beta-2}-\frac{d}{\alpha+\beta-1}\qquad(n\geqslant 1) (4.5)

for a periodic function P∈Hλ​[0,1]∩BV⁡[0,1]P\in\mathrm{H}_{\lambda}[0,1]\cap\mathrm{BV}[0,1].

Proof.

The normalised sequence

f¯​(n):=f1​(n)+2​c​nα+β−2+dα+β−1\displaystyle\bar{f}(n):=f_{1}(n)+\frac{2cn}{\alpha+\beta-2}+\frac{d}{\alpha+\beta-1} (4.6)

satisfies

Λα,β​[f¯]=((α−β)​cα+β−2−d+e)⋅𝟏n​ is odd,\displaystyle\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[\bar{f}]=\left(\frac{(\alpha-\beta)c}{\alpha+\beta-2}-d+e\right)\cdot\mathbf{1}_{n\text{ is odd}}, (4.7)

with the initial condition f¯​(1)=f1​(1)+2​cα+β−2+dα+β−1\bar{f}(1)=f_{1}(1)+\frac{2c}{\alpha+\beta-2}+\frac{d}{\alpha+\beta-1}. Thus, f¯=f2\bar{f}=f_{2}. Furthermore, f2​(n)=nϱ​P​(log2⁡n)f_{2}(n)=n^{\varrho}P(\log_{2}n) for a periodic function PP by Example 2.16. This yields (4.5). Again, the Hölder continuity and bounded variation of PP follow from Lemma 3.4. ∎

4.2 Λα,β​[f]=0\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f]=0

Example 4.4 (Generating polynomial of the sum-of-digits function).

As an immediate application of Theorem 3.6, we consider the following partial sum

f⁡(n):=∑0⩽k<nαν⁡(k)(n⩾0),f(n):=\sum_{0\leqslant k<n}\alpha^{\nu(k)}\qquad(n\geqslant 0), (4.8)

where α>0\alpha>0 and ν⁡(n)\nu(n) denotes the number of 11s in the binary expansion of nn. Such sums with various α\alpha have been encountered and studied in a large number of different contexts; see the recent survey [6] and the references therein for more information. Then by (4.8) and the recurrence relation

ν⁡(n)=ν⁡(⌊n2⌋)+𝟏n​ is odd(n⩾1),\displaystyle\nu(n)=\nu\left(\left\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\right\rfloor\right)+\mathbf{1}_{n\text{ is odd}}\qquad(n\geqslant 1), (4.9)

we see that ff satisfies Λα,1​[f]=0\Lambda_{\alpha,1}[f]=0 with f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1, or (see Example 2.15)

f​(n)=Sα,1​(n).f(n)=S_{\alpha,1}(n). (4.10)

Thus g⁡(n)≡0g(n)\equiv 0 for all nn, so (3.10) is trivial and Theorem 3.63.6 applies. Furthermore, (2.30) yields P​(t)=P0​(t)P(t)=P_{0}(t) given by (2.22), and Theorem 2.10 or Example 2.15 shows that

f⁡(n)=nlog2⁡(α+1)​P0​(log2⁡n)(n⩾1),\displaystyle f(n)=n^{\log_{2}(\alpha+1)}P_{0}(\log_{2}n)\qquad(n\geqslant 1), (4.11)

where, by Theorem 3.63.6 and (2.26),

P0​(t):=(α+1)−{t}​(1+α​φα,1​(2{t}−1))=(α+1)1−{t}​φα,1​(2{t}−1)\displaystyle P_{0}(t):=(\alpha+1)^{-\{t\}}\bigl({1+\alpha\varphi_{\alpha,1}\bigl({2^{\{t\}}-1}\bigr)}\bigr)=(\alpha+1)^{1-\{t\}}\varphi_{\alpha,1}\bigl({2^{\{t\}-1}}\bigr) (4.12)

has an absolutely convergent Fourier series for α>0\alpha>0. This extends and improves the result established in [25] for α\alpha in the range (2−1,2+1)(\sqrt{2}-1,\sqrt{2}+1), where a completely different approach was employed: instead of Zygmund’s theorem applied above (see the proof of Theorem 3.6), the proof in [25] used a theorem of Bernstein saying that a periodic function P∈HλP\in\mathrm{H}_{\lambda} with λ>12\lambda>\frac{1}{2} has an absolutely convergent Fourier series. Note that λ>12\lambda>\frac{1}{2} when α∈(2−1,2+1)\alpha\in(\sqrt{2}-1,\sqrt{2}+1).

The Fourier coefficients P0^​(k)\widehat{P_{0}}(k) are by Theorem 3.6 given by, with χk:=2​k​π​ilog⁡2\chi_{k}:=\frac{2k\pi i}{\log 2},

P0^​(k)=1log⁡2​∫011+α​φα,1​(u)(1+u)log2⁡(α+1)+χk+1​𝑑u(k∈ℤ).\widehat{P_{0}}(k)=\frac{1}{\log 2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1+\alpha\varphi_{\alpha,1}(u)}{(1+u)^{\log_{2}(\alpha+1)+\chi_{k}+1}}\,\mathrm{d}u\qquad(k\in\mathbb{Z}). (4.13)

The same type of results also hold for the recurrence Λ1,α​[f]=0\Lambda_{1,\alpha}[f]=0, the only difference being replacing the underlying interpolation function φα,1\varphi_{\alpha,1} by φ1,α\varphi_{1,\alpha}. ∎

Example 4.5 (Recurrence with minimisation or maximisation).

A class of sequences satisfying recurrences of the form

μ⁡(n)=min1⩽k⩽⌊n2⌋⁡{α​μ​(k)+β​μ​(n−k)}(n⩾2)\displaystyle\mu(n)=\min_{1\leqslant k\leqslant\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}\{\alpha\mu(k)+\beta\mu(n-k)\}\qquad(n\geqslant 2) (4.14)

with μ⁡(1)=1\mu(1)=1 was studied in [5] to solve the AND-OR Problem. It is proved there that if β⩾α\beta\geqslant\alpha are positive integers, then the minimum in (4.14) is reached at k=⌊n2⌋k=\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor, so that μ⁡(n)=f⁡(n)=Sα,β​(n)\mu(n)=f(n)=S_{\alpha,\beta}(n). In this case, Theorem 2.10 or Example 2.15 and Example 3.7 imply that μ⁡(n)=nlog2⁡(α+β)​P0​(log2⁡n)\mu(n)=n^{\log_{2}(\alpha+\beta)}P_{0}(\log_{2}n), where P0P_{0} is a periodic function with an absolutely convergent Fourier series, given by (2.22). We can extend this to the cases (i) β⩾α\beta\geqslant\alpha, β⩾1\beta\geqslant 1 and (ii) α⩾β\alpha\geqslant\beta, α+β⩽1\alpha+\beta\leqslant 1; see Appendix C.

On the other hand, it is not difficult to see that if β⩽1\beta\leqslant 1, α+β⩾1\alpha+\beta\geqslant 1, and α⩾β2\alpha\geqslant\beta^{2}, then the minimum in (4.14) is attained at k=1k=1, and we get a simple geometric expression for f⁡(n)f(n). (Apart from the trivial case α+β=1\alpha+\beta=1, when μ⁡(n)=1\mu(n)=1, these are the only (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) for which the minimum always is attained at k=1k=1.) The behaviour of the recursion (4.14) for the remaining (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) seems to be more complicated. (For example, the case 1<β<α1<\beta<\alpha.)

In Appendix C, we show in a similar manner that the solution to the corresponding recurrence with maximisation

μ⁡(n)=max1⩽k⩽⌊n2⌋⁡{α​μ​(k)+β​μ​(n−k)}(n⩾2)\displaystyle\mu(n)=\max_{1\leqslant k\leqslant\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}\{\alpha\mu(k)+\beta\mu(n-k)\}\qquad(n\geqslant 2) (4.15)

with μ⁡(1)=1\mu(1)=1 is given by μ⁡(n)=f⁡(n)=Sα,β​(n)\mu(n)=f(n)=S_{\alpha,\beta}(n) whenever α⩾β\alpha\geqslant\beta, β⩽1\beta\leqslant 1 and α+β⩾1\alpha+\beta\geqslant 1. We again obtain, by Examples 2.15 and 3.7, that f⁡(n)=nlog2⁡(α+β)​P0​(log2⁡n)f(n)=n^{\log_{2}(\alpha+\beta)}P_{0}(\log_{2}n), where P0P_{0} is the periodic function in (2.22), with an absolutely convergent Fourier series. The case α>β=1\alpha>\beta=1 of (4.15) was solved (in an equivalent form) in [32].

For more recurrences with minimisation or maximisation, see [22, 28] and the references therein. ∎

5 Applications II. α=β\alpha=\beta

We group in this section examples satisfying the recurrence Λα,α​[f]=g\Lambda_{\alpha,\alpha}[f]=g. Since the interpolating function φα,α​(t)=t\varphi_{\alpha,\alpha}(t)=t for every α>0\alpha>0, this is similar to the case α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1 treated in [27]. In particular, φα,α\varphi_{\alpha,\alpha} is linear on [0,1][0,1], and therefore we can derive in many cases a closed-form solution in terms of elementary functions. In cases when the periodic functions do not have simple explicit forms, we can often derive explicit Fourier expansions in terms of known functions such as Riemann’s or Hurwitz’s zeta functions. As the situations and analysis are very similar to the case when (α,β)=(1,1)(\alpha,\beta)=(1,1), we omit most of the details, which can be found in [27]. Note, however, one difference between the cases α>1\alpha>1 and α=1\alpha=1: as discussed in Remark 2.8, the periodic function P0​(t)P_{0}(t) in Lemma 2.7 is not continuously differentiable when α>1\alpha>1; hence, typically, the periodic function P⁡(t)P(t) in Theorem 2.10 also is not continuously differentiable.

We begin with two examples for a general α\alpha.

Example 5.1.

Consider the sum f⁡(n):=∑1⩽k<nαLkf(n):=\sum_{1\leqslant k<n}\alpha^{L_{k}}. The case α=2\alpha=2 is A063915. Since Lk=ν⁡(k)+ν0​(k)−1L_{k}=\nu(k)+\nu_{0}(k)-1 for k⩾1k\geqslant 1, we have by Example 4.7 and (4.19)

f⁡(n)=∑1⩽k<nαLk=1α​(∑0⩽k<nαν​(k)+ν0​(k)−1)=12​α−1​(Sα,α​(n)−1),\displaystyle f(n)=\sum_{1\leqslant k<n}\alpha^{L_{k}}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\biggl({\sum_{0\leqslant k<n}\alpha^{\nu(k)+\nu_{0}(k)}-1}\biggr)=\frac{1}{2\alpha-1}\bigl(S_{\alpha,\alpha}(n)-1\bigr), (5.1)

at least provided α>12\alpha>\frac{1}{2}; the result holds indeed for any α≠12\alpha\neq\frac{1}{2} since both sides are polynomials in α\alpha for fixed nn. It follows easily (cf. (4.18)), that Λα,α​[f]​(n)=g⁡(n)=1\Lambda_{\alpha,\alpha}[f](n)=g(n)=1. ∎

Λα,α​[f]=g⁡(n)=c​n+{d, if n is even;e, if n is odd.\displaystyle\Lambda_{\alpha,\alpha}[f]=g(n)=cn+\begin{cases}d,&\text{ if $n$ is even};\\ e,&\text{ if $n$ is odd}.\end{cases} (5.2)

Assume for simplicity α>1\alpha>1, so Lemma 4.3 applies. Then (4.5) yields the solution

f⁡(n)=nϱ​P​(log2⁡n)−c​nα−1−d2​α−1(n⩾1).f(n)=n^{\varrho}P(\log_{2}n)-\frac{cn}{\alpha-1}-\frac{d}{2\alpha-1}\qquad(n\geqslant 1). (5.3)

Furthermore, it follows, from the proof of Lemma 4.3, that the Fourier coefficients of the periodic function PP are given by (assuming first α>2\alpha>2 so that ϱ>2\varrho>2),

P^​(k)\displaystyle\widehat{P}(k) =1(ϱ+χk)​(ϱ+χk−1)​log⁡2​((2​α−1)​(α−1)α​f¯​(1)CLOSE\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(\varrho+\chi_{k})(\varrho+\chi_{k}-1)\log 2}\biggl(\frac{(2\alpha-1)(\alpha-1)}{\alpha}\bar{f}(1)
+(e−d)∑j⩾1((2j)−(ϱ+χk−1)−2(2j+1)−(ϱ+χk−1)+(2j+2)−(ϱ+χk−1)))\displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt+(e-d)\sum_{j\geqslant 1}\Bigl((2j)^{-(\varrho+\chi_{k}-1)}-2(2j+1)^{-(\varrho+\chi_{k}-1)}+(2j+2)^{-(\varrho+\chi_{k}-1)}\Bigr)\biggr)
=(2​α−1)​(α−1)​f​(1)+(2​α−1)​(c+e)−α​d+2​(e−d)​(2−α)​ζ​(ϱ−1+χk)α⁡(ϱ+χk)​(ϱ−1+χk)​log⁡2.\displaystyle=\frac{(2\alpha-1)(\alpha-1)f(1)+(2\alpha-1)(c+e)-\alpha d+2(e-d)(2-\alpha)\zeta(\varrho-1+\chi_{k})}{\alpha(\varrho+\chi_{k})(\varrho-1+\chi_{k})\log 2}. (5.4)

By analytic continuation (temporarily allowing complex α\alpha and ϱ\varrho), (5.4) holds for all α\alpha with α>1\alpha>1 (so ϱ>1\varrho>1), but we have to be careful when α=2\alpha=2 and thus ϱ=2\varrho=2, since then ζ\zeta has a pole at ϱ−1+χ0=1\varrho-1+\chi_{0}=1, and we have to interpret (by continuity) (2−α)​ζ​(ϱ−1+χ0)=−2​log⁡2(2-\alpha)\zeta(\varrho-1+\chi_{0})=-2\log 2. The formula simplifies when α=2\alpha=2, since then all other terms with ζ\zeta disappears. See further Example 5.4, where an explicit formula for P⁡(t)P(t) is given for α=2\alpha=2.

5.2 (α,β)=(2,2)(\alpha,\beta)=(2,2)

While most analysis here parallels that in [27], we will see that there are subtle differences in the genesis of periodic oscillations. In particular, as remarked above, the periodic function P⁡(t)P(t) is generally not continuously differentiable.

Example 5.4 (Periodic functions differentiable except at integers).

Consider the simple case when Λ2,2​[f]=c\Lambda_{2,2}[f]=c for n⩾2n\geqslant 2. Then, by Lemma 4.2, Example 2.15 and (2.22) (or directly by (2.21) and (2.22)), we deduce that

so that f⁡(n)=n2​P​(log2⁡n)−13​cf(n)=n^{2}P(\log_{2}n)-\frac{1}{3}c, where

P⁡(t)=(f⁡(1)+13​c)​P0​(t)=(f⁡(1)+13​c)​2−{t}​(3−21−{t}),P(t)=\bigl({f(1)+\tfrac{1}{3}\,c}\bigr)P_{0}(t)=\bigl({f(1)+\tfrac{1}{3}\,c}\bigr)2^{-\{t\}}(3-2^{1-\{t\}}), (5.11)

is continuously differentiable on [0,1][0,1], but not at integer tt, where the derivative P′​(t)P^{\prime}(t) has a jump.

Example 5.5 (Piecewise differentiable periodic functions).

5.5 Partial sums of Λα,0​[f]=g\Lambda_{\alpha,0}[f]=g

One simple way to generate sequences satisfying Λα,α​[f]=g\Lambda_{\alpha,\alpha}[f]=g with α=β\alpha=\beta is to consider the partial sum f⁡(n):=∑1⩽k<nh⁡(k)f(n):=\sum_{1\leqslant k<n}h(k), where Λα,0​[h]=ξ\Lambda_{\alpha,0}[h]=\xi; then

Λα,α​[f]=h⁡(1)+∑2⩽k<nξ⁡(k),\Lambda_{\alpha,\alpha}[f]=h(1)+\sum_{2\leqslant k<n}\xi(k), (5.41)

for n⩾2n\geqslant 2. Such a sum (after normalising by nn) gives the average order and more smooth asymptotics than the original sequence (which leads almost always to functions with discontinuities; see Section 6.1 and [27] for more details). For example, the partial sum of the sequence A006520 (satisfying Λ2,0​[h]=⌈12​n⌉\Lambda_{2,0}[h]=\bigl\lceil\frac{1}{2}n\bigr\rceil) gives A022560 discussed in Example 5.6 with g⁡(n)=⌊14​n2⌋g(n)=\bigl\lfloor\frac{1}{4}n^{2}\bigr\rfloor.

In a similar manner, if we define f⁡(n):=∑1⩽k⩽nh⁡(k)f(n):=\sum_{1\leqslant k\leqslant n}h(k), where Λ0,β​[h]=ξ\Lambda_{0,\beta}[h]=\xi; then

Λβ,β​[f]=(1−β)​h​(1)+∑2⩽k⩽nξ⁡(k),\Lambda_{\beta,\beta}[f]=(1-\beta)h(1)+\sum_{2\leqslant k\leqslant n}\xi(k), (5.42)

for n⩾2n\geqslant 2. Note that the equations Λα,0​[h]=ξ\Lambda_{\alpha,0}[h]=\xi and Λ0,α​[h]=ξ\Lambda_{0,\alpha}[h]=\xi are equivalent up to a shift of both hh and ξ\xi; thus it suffices to consider only one of them.

The number of such sequences on OEIS exceeds several hundred after removing sequences whose generating functions are rational (with all singularities on the unit circle). So far we discussed only OEIS sequences leading to (1,1)(1,1), (2,2)(2,2), (4,4)(4,4) and (10,10)(10,10), but in such partial sum constructions, sequences with different values of α\alpha are frequently found; see Table 11.

Example 5.10 (Partial sum of Moser-de Bruijn sequences: α⩾0\alpha\geqslant 0).

The Moser-de Bruijn sequence A000695 consists of the integers whose digits in base 4 are in {0,1}\{0,1\}; equivalently, A​000695​(n)\textup{{A}}000695(n) is obtained by reading the binary representation of nn in base 4. This sequence h⁡(n)h(n) satisfies Λ4,0[h]=𝟏n odd\Lambda_{4,0}[h]=\mathbf{1}_{n\text{ odd}}. Hence, (5.41) shows that the partial sum f⁡(n):=∑k<nh⁡(n)f(n):=\sum_{k<n}h(n) satisfies

Λ4,4​[f]​(n)=⌊n2⌋,n⩾2.\Lambda_{4,4}[f](n)=\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor,\qquad n\geqslant 2. (5.43)

for any α\alpha and any σ>max⁡(ϱ−1,0)\sigma>\max(\varrho-1,0). This provides by standard methods an alternative proof of several of the results above.

In particular, when α=2\alpha=2, we have f⁡(n)=(n2)f(n)=\binom{n}{2} and P⁡(t)=12P(t)=\frac{1}{2}. When α=1\alpha=1, we can use Theorem A.2 and conclude that

where P⁡(t)P(t) is the Trollope–Delange fractal function (see [6, 12]):
