Convergence of Fourier series.

For a fixed real σ\sigma, and all real tt with |t|⩾2|t|\geqslant 2, it is known that

|ζ⁡(σ+i​t)|={Θ⁡(|t|12−σ),σ<0,O⁡(|t|12​log⁡|t|),σ=0,O⁡(|t|12−σ2),0<σ<1,O⁡(log⁡|t|),σ=1,Θ⁡(1),σ>1,|\zeta(\sigma+it)|=\begin{cases}\Theta(|t|^{\frac{1}{2}-\sigma}),&\sigma<0,\\ O(|t|^{\frac{1}{2}}\log|t|),&\sigma=0,\\ O\bigl(|t|^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sigma}{2}}\bigr),&0<\sigma<1,\\ O(\log|t|),&\sigma=1,\\ \Theta(1),&\sigma>1,\end{cases} (5.55)

see, e.g., [39, Chapter 5] or [29, Section 1.5]. (Stronger results are known for 0⩽σ⩽10\leqslant\sigma\leqslant 1; the best exponents are still not known for 0<σ<10<\sigma<1.) Hence, the Fourier series in (5.50) and (5.54) are absolutely convergent if and only if ϱ>12\varrho>\frac{1}{2}, i.e., if α>22\alpha>\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}. Thus, if 12<α<22\frac{1}{2}<\alpha<\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, then the Fourier series is not absolutely convergent. (As a check, we note that (5.55) verifies that the Fourier coefficients are in ℓ2\ell^{2} for every α>12\alpha>\frac{1}{2} (ϱ>0\varrho>0), which is obvious from Parseval’s formula. On the other hand, for 0<α⩽120<\alpha\leqslant\frac{1}{2}, (5.50) is not the Fourier series of any L2L^{2} function.) ∎

6 Extension to nonpositive α\alpha or β\beta

We have so far considered the recurrence (1.1), or, equivalently (2.1), with α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0. Here we discuss rather briefly α\alpha and β\beta with other sign combinations. The case α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0 is trivial, with (1.1) reduced to f⁡(n)=g⁡(n)f(n)=g(n), and is ignored in the sequel.

6.1 Recurrences with α=0\alpha=0 or β=0\beta=0

The situation when α\alpha or β\beta equals zero is very similar to the special cases (α,β)=(2,0)(\alpha,\beta)=(2,0) and (0,2)(0,2) discussed in our previous paper [27], and we give only some brief comments. Such sequences abound in OEIS; see Table 11 for a few examples of one kind.

For any α≠0\alpha\neq 0, (2.4) is solved by φα,0​(t)=0\varphi_{\alpha,0}(t)=0, t∈[0,1)t\in[0,1), and thus (2.2) yields f⁡(x)=f⁡(⌊x⌋)f(x)=f(\lfloor x\rfloor). Similarly, for β≠0\beta\neq 0, φ0,β​(t)=1\varphi_{0,\beta}(t)=1, t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1], and thus f⁡(x)=f⁡(⌈x⌉)f(x)=f(\lceil x\rceil). The main difference from the case α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0 is that now φ\varphi is discontinuous (at an endpoint), and thus f⁡(x)f(x) is discontinuous except in trivial cases, In the cases (α,0)(\alpha,0) with α>0\alpha>0 and (0,β)(0,\beta) with β>0\beta>0, it is easily verified that Theorem 2.10 holds with modifications similar to the special cases in [27, Theorems 4 and 5]; note that the periodic function P⁡(t)P(t) now is discontinuous except in trivial cases. If α<0\alpha<0 or β<0\beta<0, this holds with further modifications as in Section 6.2 below. We omit the details.

6.2 Recurrences with both α\alpha and β\beta negative

In this section, we consider the case when α\alpha and β\beta both are negative; see Table 12 for a few examples from OEIS (discussed below). We thus assume the recurrence (1.1), or, equivalently, (2.1) with α,β<0\alpha,\beta<0. In this case we define

ϱ:=log2⁡(|α|+|β|).\displaystyle\varrho:=\log_{2}(|\alpha|+|\beta|). (6.1)

Thus α+β=−2ϱ\alpha+\beta=-2^{\varrho}. As above, we define g⁡(1):=0g(1):=0. We also extend the definition of φα,β​(t)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(t) to negative values of α,β\alpha,\beta by φα,β​(t):=φ|α|,|β|​(t)\varphi_{\alpha,\beta}(t):=\varphi_{|\alpha|,|\beta|}(t), and note that then (2.4) holds. The proof of Lemma 2.1 applies, mutatis mutandis, and shows that (2.3) holds in this case too. It follows that the theory developed in Sections 2–3 extends to this case, but with an important modification.

We say that a function P⁡(t)P(t) on ℝ\mathbb{R} is 11-antiperiodic if P⁡(t+1)=−P⁡(t)P(t+1)=-P(t) for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}. In other words, P⁡(t)P(t) is 11-antiperiodic if and only if eπ​i​t​P​(t)e^{\pi it}P(t) is 11-periodic.

Note that every 11-antiperiodic function is 22-periodic. Moreover, a 11-antiperiodic function that is integrable on [0,1][0,1] (and thus on any compact interval) has a Fourier series that can be written

P⁡(t)∼∑k∈ℤP^​(k+12)​e(2​k+1)​π​i​t.\displaystyle P(t)\sim\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\widehat{P}(k+\tfrac{1}{2})e^{(2k+1)\pi it}. (6.2)

We collect the most important results in the following theorem, leaving the others in Sections 2–3 to the reader.

Theorem 6.1.

Suppose that α,β<0\alpha,\beta<0, and let ϱ:=log2(|α|+β|)\varrho:=\log_{2}(|\alpha|+\beta|). Then Theorem 2.10 holds with the modifications that 11-periodic is replaced by 11-antiperiodic, and that (2.28) and (2.30) are replaced by

P0​(t):=(−1)⌊t⌋​(1+(α+β−1)​φ​(2{t}−1))​2−ϱ​{t}.P_{0}\left(t\right):=(-1)^{\lfloor t\rfloor}\bigl(1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi\bigl({2^{\{t\}}-1}\bigr)\bigr)2^{-\varrho\{t\}}. (6.5)

P^​(k+12)=1log⁡2​∫1∞g⁡(u)uϱ+χk′+1​𝑑u+f⁡(1)log⁡2​∫011+(α+β−1)​φ​(u)(1+u)ϱ+χk′+1​𝑑u,\widehat{P}(k+\tfrac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{\log 2}\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{g(u)}{u^{\varrho+\chi^{\prime}_{k}+1}}\,\mathrm{d}u+\frac{f(1)}{\log 2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi(u)}{(1+u)^{\varrho+\chi^{\prime}_{k}+1}}\,\mathrm{d}u, (6.6)

P^​(k+12)\displaystyle\widehat{P}(k+\tfrac{1}{2}) =1(ϱ+χk′)​(ϱ−1+χk′)​log⁡2​(D⁡(ϱ−1+χk′)+(2​α−1)​(α−1)α​f​(1)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(\varrho+\chi^{\prime}_{k})(\varrho-1+\chi^{\prime}_{k})\log 2}\Bigl(D(\varrho-1+\chi^{\prime}_{k})+\frac{(2\alpha-1)(\alpha-1)}{\alpha}f(1)\Bigr), (6.8)

Proof.

The proof follows by the same arguments used in Sections 2–3, with minor modifications. In particular, Lemma 2.7 and Propositions 2.11–2.12 hold with P0P_{0} and QQ as above, 11-periodic replaced by 11-antiperiodic, and extra factors (−1)k(-1)^{k} or (−1)m(-1)^{m} in the sums in (2.21), (2.32), (2.33) and in the definition of Gm​(x)G_{m}(x). Note that (2.35) now becomes

Remark 6.2.

Thus P⁡(log2⁡n)P(\log_{2}n) in our formulas now is an 11-antiperiodic function of log2⁡n\log_{2}n, which implies that it is a 22-periodic function of log2⁡n\log_{2}n, or, equivalently, a 11-periodic function of 12​log2​n=log4⁡n\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}n=\log_{4}n. ∎

Remark 6.3.

Most of the formulas in Sections 2–3 hold verbatim for α,β<0\alpha,\beta<0 if we instead replace ϱ\varrho by the complex logarithm ϱ𝖼:=log2⁡(α+β)=ϱ+π​i/log⁡2\varrho_{\mathsf{c}}:=\log_{2}(\alpha+\beta)=\varrho+\pi i/\log 2. However, this seems less convenient for applications. ∎

6.3 Recurrences with either α\alpha or β\beta negative

There are many examples in OEIS of sequences satisfying Λα,β​[f]=g\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f]=g with α​β<0\alpha\beta<0, i.e., one of α\alpha and β\beta is positive and the other is negative. In this case, we can still define φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) for dyadic rationals t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] by (2.11) (and it has to have this value), but since now |α+β|<|α|,|β||\alpha+\beta|<|\alpha|,|\beta|, this function is unbounded in every interval, and thus cannot be extended to a continuous function (or any other reasonable function) on [0,1][0,1]. Hence our methods break down, and we have no general theorem in this case. Moreover, we do not expect any simple asymptotics in general, which is illustrated by the following example.

Example 6.8.

Consider again f​(n)=Sα,β​(n)f(n)=S_{\alpha,\beta}(n) defined by Λα,β​[f]​(n)=0\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f](n)=0 and f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1. In particular, we have

f⁡(2​n)=(α+β)​f​(n),n⩾1.\displaystyle f(2n)=(\alpha+\beta)f(n),\qquad n\geqslant 1. (6.23)

f⁡(n+1)−f⁡(n)=(α+β−1)​αν⁡(n)−1​βν0​(n).\displaystyle f(n+1)-f(n)=(\alpha+\beta-1)\alpha^{\nu(n)-1}\beta^{\nu_{0}(n)}. (6.24)

By (6.23) and (6.24), we have, for example,

f⁡(2k)\displaystyle f(2^{k}) =(α+β)k,\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)^{k}, k⩾0,\displaystyle k\geqslant 0, (6.25)
f⁡(2k−1)\displaystyle f(2^{k}-1) =(α+β)k−(α+β−1)​αk−1,\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)^{k}-(\alpha+\beta-1)\alpha^{k-1}, k⩾1,\displaystyle k\geqslant 1, (6.26)
f⁡(2k+1)\displaystyle f(2^{k}+1) =(α+β)k+(α+β−1)​βk,\displaystyle=(\alpha+\beta)^{k}+(\alpha+\beta-1)\beta^{k}, k⩾0.\displaystyle k\geqslant 0. (6.27)

Consider, for definiteness, the case α>0>β\alpha>0>\beta with |α|⩾|β||\alpha|\geqslant|\beta|. Then 0⩽α+β<α0\leqslant\alpha+\beta<\alpha. Assume also α+β≠1\alpha+\beta\neq 1. (Otherwise, Sα,β​(n)=1S_{\alpha,\beta}(n)=1 for all nn.) We see from (6.26) that |f⁡(n)||f(n)| may be of the order αlog2⁡n=nlog2⁡α\alpha^{\log_{2}n}=n^{\log_{2}\alpha}, although (6.25) shows that |f⁡(n)||f(n)| also may be much smaller. In fact, it is easily shown by induction using (6.23)–(6.24) that |f⁡(n)|⩽C​αLn|f(n)|\leqslant C\alpha^{L_{n}} for some constant CC (depending on α\alpha and β\beta) and all nn. Hence, f~​(n):=n−log2⁡α​f​(n)\widetilde{f}(n):=n^{-\log_{2}\alpha}f(n) is bounded. However, f~​(n)\widetilde{f}(n) does not seem to have any simple asymptotic approximations, as the following arguments show.

First, (6.25) and (6.26) show that f~​(n)\widetilde{f}(n) have infinitely many jumps with size of order 1. More precisely, it can be seen from (6.24) that for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that every interval [N,(1+ε)​N][N,(1+\varepsilon)N] with N⩾1N\geqslant 1 contains some nn such that the jump |f~​(n+1)−f~​(n)|>δ|\widetilde{f}(n+1)-\widetilde{f}(n)|>\delta.

Secondly, we cannot have |f⁡(n)|=nlog2⁡α​(P⁡(log2⁡n)+o⁡(1))|f(n)|=n^{\log_{2}\alpha}\bigl(P(\log_{2}n)+o(1)\bigr) for any 11-periodic function P⁡(t)P(t), because then substituting 2​n2n would give |f⁡(2​n)|=α​nlog2⁡α​(P⁡(log2⁡n)+o⁡(1))|f(2n)|=\alpha n^{\log_{2}\alpha}\bigl(P(\log_{2}n)+o(1)\bigr), while (6.23) would imply |f⁡(2​n)|=(α+β)​nlog2⁡α​(P⁡(log2⁡n)+o⁡(1))|f(2n)|=(\alpha+\beta)n^{\log_{2}\alpha}\bigl(P(\log_{2}n)+o(1)\bigr), and together these imply P⁡(log2⁡n)=o⁡(1)P(\log_{2}n)=o(1), so we would have f⁡(n)=o⁡(nlog2⁡α)f(n)=o(n^{\log_{2}\alpha}), which contradicts (6.26). ∎

There are many OEIS sequences in this category too, and most of them have α+β=0\alpha+\beta=0. We do not discuss these examples further since we have nothing new to add by our methods, but just mention a prototype sequence A115384, the partial sum of Thue-Morse sequence (A010060, the parity of the dyadic valuation), which satisfies Λ−1,1​[f]=⌊n2⌋\Lambda_{-1,1}[f]=\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor with f⁡(1)=0f(1)=0. The exact solution is given by f⁡(n)=⌊n2⌋+14​(1−(−1)n)​(1+(−1)ν⁡(n−1))f(n)=\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor+\frac{1}{4}(1-(-1)^{n})(1+(-1)^{\nu(n-1)}), where the last term indicates why there is no simple smooth function providing good asymptotic approximation to f⁡(n)−n2f(n)-\frac{n}{2}. See also other related sequences A076826, A159481, A173209 and A245710, which have a very similar behaviour.

7 Extension from binary to qq-ary

We consider briefly the more general recurrence

f⁡(n)=∑0⩽j<qαj​f​(⌊n+jq⌋)+g⁡(n)(n⩾q),\displaystyle f(n)=\sum_{0\leqslant j<q}\alpha_{j}f\bigl({\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{n+j}{q}\bigr\rfloor}\bigr)+g(n)\qquad(n\geqslant q), (7.1)

for some integer q⩾2q\geqslant 2 and qq given constants α0,…,αq−1\alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{q-1}; note that the case q=2q=2 corresponds to (1.1). We now require g⁡(n)g(n) for n⩾qn\geqslant q and the initial values {f⁡(1),…,f⁡(q−1)}\{f(1),\dots,f(q-1)\}.

Just as the recurrence (1.1), for example, occurs naturally in many combinatorial and algorithmic contexts where a problem is split into two halves, the generalisation (7.1) occurs typically in divide-and-conquer context or recursive structures where we instead divide the source problem into qq subproblems of sizes as evenly as possible.

The case α0=⋯=αq−1=1\alpha_{0}=\dots=\alpha_{q-1}=1 was discussed in [27] with several examples from the literature and OEIS. We can similarly extend the method of Section 2 to treat the general recursion (7.1) under suitable conditions. We assume that αj\alpha_{j} are real with

max0⩽j<q⁡|αj|<A:=∑0⩽j<qαj.\displaystyle\max_{0\leqslant j<q}|\alpha_{j}|<A:=\sum_{0\leqslant j<q}\alpha_{j}. (7.2)

Note that (7.2) holds in the standard case when all αj>0\alpha_{j}>0; it also holds, more generally, if αj⩾0\alpha_{j}\geqslant 0 for all jj and at least two αj\alpha_{j} are non-zero.

Lemma 7.1.

Assume (7.2). Then there exists a unique continuous function φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) on [0,1][0,1] such that φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0, φ⁡(1)=1\varphi(1)=1, and for j=0,…,q−1j=0,\dots,q-1,

φ⁡(t)=αq−1−jA​φ​(q​t−j)+∑q−j⩽i<qαiA,ifjq⩽t⩽j+1q.\displaystyle\varphi(t)=\frac{\alpha_{q-1-j}}{A}\varphi(qt-j)+\frac{\sum_{q-j\leqslant i<q}\alpha_{i}}{A},\qquad\text{if}\quad\frac{j}{q}\leqslant t\leqslant\frac{j+1}{q}. (7.3)

Moreover, if αj⩾0\alpha_{j}\geqslant 0 for all jj, then φ\varphi is strictly increasing.

Proof.

This follows with only notational changes as in our third proof of Lemma 2.3 based on the recursive construction (2.16); we obtain by an analogue of (2.16) a sequence of continuous functions φk\varphi_{k} that, using (7.2), converge uniformly to a function φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) satisfying (7.3). ∎

We then extend f⁡(n)f(n) and g⁡(n)g(n) to functions of a real variable x⩾1x\geqslant 1 by (2.2) as before, and it is easily verified that (2.3) generalises to

f⁡(x)=A​f​(xq)+g⁡(x),x⩾q.\displaystyle f(x)=Af\left(\frac{x}{q}\right)+g(x),\qquad x\geqslant q. (7.4)

We may now argue as in Section 2 and prove extensions of Theorem 2.10 and its corollaries for the recursion (7.1). We now define

ϱ:=logq⁡A=log⁡(∑0⩽j<qαj).\displaystyle\varrho:=\log_{q}A=\log\Bigl(\sum_{0\leqslant j<q}\alpha_{j}\Bigr). (7.5)

The simplest situation is when g⁡(n)=O⁡(nϱ−ε)g(n)=O(n^{\varrho-\varepsilon}) for some ε>0\varepsilon>0; then

f⁡(x)=xϱ​P​(logq⁡x)−Q⁡(x),x⩾1,\displaystyle f(x)=x^{\varrho}P(\log_{q}x)-Q(x),\qquad x\geqslant 1, (7.6)

where P⁡(t)P(t) is a continuous 11-periodic function, and

Q⁡(x):=∑m⩾1q−ϱ​m​g​(qm​x)=o⁡(xϱ).\displaystyle Q(x):=\sum_{m\geqslant 1}q^{-\varrho m}g(q^{m}x)=o(x^{\varrho}). (7.7)

We leave further details to the reader and content ourselves with the discussion of two classes of examples.

7.1 Binomial coefficients not divisible by a prime qq

Let f⁡(n)f(n) denote the number of binomial coefficients (mk)\binom{m}{k}, 0⩽k⩽m<n0\leqslant k\leqslant m<n, that are not divisible by a given prime qq. This sequence has a long history, at least dating back to Fine’s [17] observation that almost all binomial coefficients are even; see, e.g., [8] and the references therein. It equals A006046 (see Example 4.9) when q=2q=2. The case q=3q=3 corresponds to A006048, while q=5q=5 gives A194458. We then deduce the recurrence

f⁡(n)=∑0⩽j<q(q−j)​f​(⌊n+jq⌋),f(n)=\sum_{0\leqslant j<q}(q-j)f\bigl({\lfloor\tfrac{n+j}{q}\rfloor}\bigr), (7.8)

with f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and f⁡(1)=1f(1)=1. This is (7.1) with αj=q−j\alpha_{j}=q-j and g⁡(n)=0g(n)=0; furthermore, in this example (7.8) holds for all n⩾0n\geqslant 0. We have A=(q+12)A=\binom{q+1}{2} and ϱ:=logq⁡A\varrho:=\log_{q}A. Stein [37] proved that

1A⩽f⁡(n)nϱ⩽1,\frac{1}{A}\leqslant\frac{f(n)}{n^{\varrho}}\leqslant 1, (7.9)

and extended f⁡(n)f(n) to a continuous function f⁡(x)f(x); see [21, 40, 42] for finer lower bounds. Our general approach yields the same continuous extension f⁡(x)f(x) as in [37]; we obtain (by (7.6))

f⁡(n)nϱ=P⁡(logq⁡n)(n⩾1),\frac{f(n)}{n^{\varrho}}=P(\log_{q}n)\qquad(n\geqslant 1), (7.10)

where P⁡(t):=A−{t}​f​(q{t})P(t):=A^{-\{t\}}f(q^{\{t\}}) is a continuous 11-periodic function. Moreover, since (7.8) holds for all n⩾1n\geqslant 1, it is easily verified (using (7.3)) that f⁡(x)=A​φ​(x/q)f(x)=A\varphi(x/q) for x∈[1,q]x\in[1,q], and thus

P⁡(t)=A1−{t}​φ​(q{t}−1).P(t)=A^{1-\{t\}}\varphi(q^{\{t\}-1}). (7.11)

(Cf. Remark 2.9 for a similar simplification, for related reasons.) Here φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) satisfies φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0, φ⁡(1)=1\varphi(1)=1, and for 0⩽j<q0\leqslant j<q,

φ⁡(t)=j+1A​φ​({q​t})+(j+12)A,ifjq⩽t⩽j+1q.\varphi(t)=\frac{j+1}{A}\varphi(\{qt\})+\frac{\binom{j+1}{2}}{A},\qquad\text{if}\quad\frac{j}{q}\leqslant t\leqslant\frac{j+1}{q}. (7.12)

By (7.9) or (7.10), almost all binomial coefficients are divisible by any given prime qq because

ϱ=logq⁡(q+1)−logq⁡2+1<2.\varrho=\log_{q}(q+1)-\log_{q}2+1<2. (7.13)

Alternatively, it is known [8] that

f⁡(n)=12​∑0⩽j⩽s(p+12)j​bj​∏j⩽i⩽s(bi+1),f(n)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{0\leqslant j\leqslant s}{\binom{p+1}{2}}^{j}b_{j}\prod_{j\leqslant i\leqslant s}(b_{i}+1), (7.14)

when n=b0+b1q+⋯bsqsn=b_{0}+b_{1}q+\cdots b_{s}q^{s} with 0⩽bj<q0\leqslant b_{j}<q and s=⌊logq⁡n⌋s=\lfloor\log_{q}n\rfloor, from which we can obtain an alternative representation for the periodic function PP. Also the generating function [37]

∑n⩾0f⁡(n)​zn=z1−z​∏k⩾0∑0⩽j<q(j+1)​zj⋅qk,\sum_{n\geqslant 0}f(n)z^{n}=\frac{z}{1-z}\prod_{k\geqslant 0}\sum_{0\leqslant j<q}(j+1)z^{j\cdot q^{k}}, (7.15)

is helpful in applying the Mellin transform approach; see [20, 24, 25].

The more general problem of the number of multinomial coefficients (mj1,…,jd)\binom{m}{j_{1},\dots,j_{d}} not divisible by a prime qq, for 0⩽m<n0\leqslant m<n and j1+⋯+jd=mj_{1}+\cdots+j_{d}=m, j1,…,jd⩾0j_{1},\dots,j_{d}\geqslant 0, where d⩾1d\geqslant 1 is given (see [7, 8, 40]) can be similarly dealt with. This number satisfies the recurrence

f⁡(n)=∑0⩽j<q(q−j+d−2d−1)​f​(⌊n+jq⌋);f(n)=\sum_{0\leqslant j<q}\binom{q-j+d-2}{d-1}f\Bigl({\Bigl\lfloor\frac{n+j}{q}\Bigr\rfloor}\Bigr); (7.16)

we then deduce, by (7.6), the identity f⁡(n)=nϱ​P​(logq⁡n)f(n)=n^{\varrho}P(\log_{q}n), n⩾1n\geqslant 1, for some continuous periodic function PP with ϱ=logq⁡(q+d−1d)\varrho=\log_{q}\binom{q+d-1}{d}.

7.2 Generating polynomial of Gray codes

Gray codes of integers are strings of binary words in which neighboring code words differ by one bit only; we already discussed some properties of the binary reflected Gray codes in Examples 5.6 and 5.8. Here, we consider a simple extended version of binary Gray codes to qq-ary ones (non-reflected); see [9, 36]. The construction is as follows. If

n=∑0⩽j⩽sκj​qj,(0⩽κj<q),n=\sum_{0\leqslant j\leqslant s}\kappa_{j}q^{j},\qquad(0\leqslant\kappa_{j}<q), (7.17)

then the Gray code of nn is given by (κs′,…,κ0′)(\kappa_{s}^{\prime},\dots,\kappa_{0}^{\prime}), where κs′=κs\kappa_{s}^{\prime}=\kappa_{s} and

κj′:=(κj−κj+1)modq(0⩽j<s).\kappa_{j}^{\prime}:=(\kappa_{j}-\kappa_{j+1})\bmod q\qquad(0\leqslant j<s). (7.18)

For simplicity, we consider the number of nonzero digits γ⁡(n):=∑0⩽j⩽s𝟏κj′>0\gamma(n):=\sum_{0\leqslant j\leqslant s}\mathbf{1}_{\kappa_{j}^{\prime}>0} in this Gray code representation of nn; other quantities such as the sum of digits ∑0⩽j⩽sκj′\sum_{0\leqslant j\leqslant s}\kappa_{j}^{\prime} can be considered similarly (a sketch given below). Then by the recurrence

γ⁡(q​k+j)=γ⁡(k)+{0,if ​kmodq≡j;1,otherwise,\gamma(qk+j)=\gamma(k)+\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }k\bmod q\equiv j;\\ 1,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (7.19)

for 0⩽j<q0\leqslant j<q, we deduce that the generating polynomial f⁡(n):=∑0⩽k<nαγ⁡(k)f(n):=\sum_{0\leqslant k<n}\alpha^{\gamma(k)} of γ⁡(n)\gamma(n) satisfies

f⁡(n)=f⁡(⌊nq⌋)+α​∑1⩽j<qf⁡(⌊n+jq⌋)+g⁡(n),f(n)=f\bigl({\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{n}{q}\bigr\rfloor}\bigr)+\alpha\sum_{1\leqslant j<q}f\bigl({\bigl\lfloor\tfrac{n+j}{q}\bigr\rfloor}\bigr)+g(n), (7.20)

where gg can be expressed as

g⁡(q2​k+q​r+j)=(1−α)​αγ⁡(q​k+r)+1(k⩾0),\displaystyle g(q^{2}k+qr+j)=(1-\alpha)\alpha^{\gamma(qk+r)+1}\qquad(k\geqslant 0), (7.21)

for 0⩽r⩽q−20\leqslant r\leqslant q-2 and r+1⩽j⩽q−1r+1\leqslant j\leqslant q-1, and g⁡(n)=0g(n)=0 for all other values of nn. Alternatively, in terms of qq-ary expansion, the nonzero g⁡(n)g(n), 0⩽n<q20\leqslant n<q^{2}, occurs when n=(κ1,κ0)qn=(\kappa_{1},\kappa_{0})_{q} is of the form:

(0,1)q,(0,2)q,(0,3)q,(0,4)q,…,(0,q−1)q(0,1)_{q},(0,2)_{q},(0,3)_{q},(0,4)_{q},\dots,(0,q-1)_{q}

Appendix A Mellin transforms

Mellin transforms are another useful techniques in analysing divide-and-conquer recurrences; see [18, 19, 20, 25, 28] and the references therein for more information. Up to now most of the tools we adopt to solve (1.1) are direct and elementary in nature; it is however possible to apply Mellin transforms for a more effective characterisation of the underlying periodic oscillations, notably calculations of the Fourier coefficients, as already observed before in the literature (although an analytic approach often requires stronger conditions).

Let again α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, and ϱ:=log2⁡(α+β)\varrho:=\log_{2}(\alpha+\beta), and assume that f⁡(n)f(n) and g⁡(n)g(n) satisfy the recursion (1.1). Extend again ff and gg to [1,∞)[1,\infty) by (2.2), with g⁡(1):=0g(1):=0, and define f⁡(x):=g⁡(x):=0f(x):=g(x):=0 for x∈[0,1)x\in[0,1). Denote the Mellin transform of f⁡(x)f(x) by f∗​(s)f^{*}(s):

f∗​(s):=∫0∞f⁡(x)​xs−1​𝑑x=∫1∞f⁡(x)​xs−1​𝑑x,\displaystyle f^{*}(s):=\int_{0}^{\infty}f(x)x^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_{1}^{\infty}f(x)x^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}x, (A.1)

for all complex ss such that the integral is absolutely convergent, and similarly for g∗​(s)g^{*}(s). If f⁡(n)=O⁡(nc)f(n)=O(n^{c}) for large nn and some real cc, then f∗​(s)f^{*}(s) exists at least in the half-plane ℜ⁡s<−c\Re s<-c, and is analytic there. If f∗​(s)f^{*}(s) or g∗​(s)g^{*}(s) extends meromorphically to a larger domain, we use the same notation there.

Assume that f∗​(s)f^{*}(s) and g∗​(s)g^{*}(s) exist. Then (2.3) implies that

f∗​(s)\displaystyle f^{*}(s) =∫12f⁡(x)​xs−1​𝑑x+∫2∞(2ϱ​f​(x2)+g⁡(x))​xs−1​𝑑x\displaystyle=\int_{1}^{2}f(x)x^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_{2}^{\infty}\Bigl(2^{\varrho}f\Bigl(\frac{x}{2}\Bigr)+g(x)\Bigr)x^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}x
=∫12(f⁡(x)−g⁡(x))​xs−1​𝑑x+2ϱ+s​f∗​(s)+g∗​(s).\displaystyle=\int_{1}^{2}\bigl(f(x)-g(x)\bigr)x^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}x+2^{\varrho+s}f^{*}(s)+g^{*}(s). (A.2)

Furthermore, (2.21) or (2.23) shows that if 1⩽x<21\leqslant x<2, then f⁡(x)−g⁡(x)=f⁡(1)​P0​(log2⁡x)​xϱf(x)-g(x)=f(1)P_{0}(\log_{2}x)x^{\varrho}. Hence, recalling the definition (2.22),

∫12(f⁡(x)−g⁡(x))​xs−1​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\bigl(f(x)-g(x)\bigr)x^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}x =f⁡(1)​∫12P0​(log2⁡x)​xϱ+s−1​𝑑x\displaystyle=f(1)\int_{1}^{2}P_{0}(\log_{2}x)x^{\varrho+s-1}\,\mathrm{d}x
=f⁡(1)​∫12(1+(2ϱ−1)​φ​(x−1))​xs−1​𝑑x.\displaystyle=f(1)\int_{1}^{2}\left(1+(2^{\varrho}-1)\varphi\left(x-1\right)\right)x^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}x. (A.3)

Substituting this into (A.2) yields

(1−2ϱ+s)​f∗​(s)=g∗​(s)+f⁡(1)​∫01(1+(2ϱ−1)​φ​(u))​(1+u)s−1​𝑑u.\displaystyle\left(1-2^{\varrho+s}\right)f^{*}(s)=g^{*}(s)+f(1)\int_{0}^{1}\left(1+(2^{\varrho}-1)\varphi(u)\right)(1+u)^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}u. (A.4)

Note that the right-hand side of (3.25) equals, apart from a factor 1log⁡2\frac{1}{\log 2}, the right-hand side of (A.4) at s=−ϱ−χks=-\varrho-\chi_{k}. On the other hand, for such ss, the left-hand side factor 1−2ϱ+s1-2^{\varrho+s} equals zero. Hence, combining (A.4) and Theorem 3.63.6 yields the following (see [19] for more information).

Lemma A.1.

If g⁡(n)=O⁡(nϱ−ε)g(n)=O(n^{\varrho-\varepsilon}) for some ε>0\varepsilon>0, then g∗​(s)g^{*}(s) is analytic in (at least) the half-plane ℜ⁡s<−ϱ+ε\Re s<-\varrho+\varepsilon, and f∗​(s)f^{*}(s) is meromorphic in the same half-plane with only simple poles, which are at −ϱ−χk=−ϱ−2​k​π​ilog⁡2-\varrho-\chi_{k}=-\varrho-\frac{2k\pi i}{\log 2} for some k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}. Furthermore, Theorem 3.63.6 applies, and

P^​(k)=−Res⁡[f∗​(s);s=−ϱ−χk].\displaystyle\widehat{P}(k)=-\operatorname{Res}\left[f^{*}(s);s=-\varrho-\chi_{k}\right]. (A.5)

We do not claim that every −ϱ−χk-\varrho-\chi_{k} actually is a pole. In fact, by (A.5), −ϱ−χk-\varrho-\chi_{k} is a pole of f∗​(s)f^{*}(s) if and only if P^​(k)≠0\widehat{P}(k)\neq 0.

For a better demonstration of the approach, we study the case when g⁡(n)∼nϱg(n)\sim n^{\varrho}, and thus Theorem 2.10 does not directly apply (although readily amenable) due to an extra logarithmic leading term in the asymptotic approximation of f⁡(n)f(n). For a meromorphic function F⁡(z)F(z), let F​(s)finF(s)_{\mathrm{fin}} denote finite value (or the constant term) in the Laurent series expansion at z=sz=s; thus F​(s)fin=F⁡(s)F(s)_{\mathrm{fin}}=F(s) when the latter is finite.

Theorem A.2.

Assume that g⁡(n)=nϱ+g0​(n)g(n)=n^{\varrho}+g_{0}(n), where g0​(n)=O⁡(nϱ−ε)g_{0}(n)=O(n^{\varrho-\varepsilon}) for some ε>0\varepsilon>0. Then

f⁡(n)=nϱ​log2​n+nϱ​P​(log2⁡n)−Q⁡(n),n⩾1,f(n)=n^{\varrho}\log_{2}n+n^{\varrho}P(\log_{2}n)-Q(n),\qquad n\geqslant 1, (A.6)

where (as in Theorem 2.10) P⁡(t)P(t) is a continuous 11-periodic function and Q⁡(n)=o⁡(nϱ)Q(n)=o\left(n^{\varrho}\right) as n→∞n\to\infty. The Fourier coefficients of P⁡(t)P(t) are given by

P^​(k)=f⁡(1)log⁡2​∫011+(α+β−1)​φ​(u)(1+u)ϱ+χk+1​𝑑u+{1log⁡2​g∗​(−ϱ−χk),k≠0,1log⁡2​g∗​(−ϱ)fin+12,k=0,\widehat{P}(k)=\frac{f(1)}{\log 2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\varphi(u)}{(1+u)^{\varrho+\chi_{k}+1}}\,\mathrm{d}u+\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\log 2}g^{*}(-\varrho-\chi_{k}),&k\neq 0,\\ \frac{1}{\log 2}g^{*}(-\varrho)_{\mathrm{fin}}+\frac{1}{2},&k=0,\end{cases} (A.7)

where g∗​(s)g^{*}(s) is meromorphic in ℜ⁡s<−ϱ+(ε∧1)\Re s<-\varrho+(\varepsilon\wedge 1) with a sole simple pole at s=−ϱs=-\varrho. In particular, (3.25) holds for k≠0k\neq 0.

If, moreover, g⁡(n)=nϱg(n)=n^{\varrho} for even n⩾2n\geqslant 2 (i.e., g0​(2​m)=0g_{0}(2m)=0), then Q⁡(n)=0Q(n)=0 for n⩾1n\geqslant 1.

Proof.

Assume, without loss of generality, ε<1\varepsilon<1. The assumption and (2.2) then imply that we have, for n⩾1n\geqslant 1 and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1],

|g⁡(n+t)−g⁡(n)|\displaystyle|g(n+t)-g(n)| ⩽|g⁡(n+1)−g⁡(n)|=|(n+1)ϱ−nϱ+g0​(n+1)−g0​(n)|\displaystyle\leqslant|g(n+1)-g(n)|=|(n+1)^{\varrho}-n^{\varrho}+g_{0}(n+1)-g_{0}(n)|
=O⁡(nϱ−ε),\displaystyle=O\bigl(n^{\varrho-\varepsilon}\bigr), (A.8)

which together with a Taylor expansion of (n+t)s−1(n+t)^{s-1} yields, for ℜ⁡s<−ϱ\Re s<-\varrho,

g∗​(s)\displaystyle g^{*}(s) =∑n⩾1∫01g⁡(n+t)​(n+t)s−1​𝑑t=∑n⩾1(g⁡(n)​ns−1+O⁡(nϱ+ℜ⁡s−1−ε))\displaystyle=\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\int_{0}^{1}g(n+t)(n+t)^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}t=\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\Bigl(g(n)n^{s-1}+O\bigl(n^{\varrho+\Re s-1-\varepsilon}\bigr)\Bigr)
=∑n⩾1nϱ+s−1+∑⩾1O⁡(nϱ+ℜ⁡s−1−ε)\displaystyle=\sum_{n\geqslant 1}n^{\varrho+s-1}+\sum_{\geqslant 1}O\bigl(n^{\varrho+\Re s-1-\varepsilon}\bigr)
=ζ⁡(1−ϱ−s)+∑n⩾1O⁡(nϱ+ℜ⁡s−1−ε).\displaystyle=\zeta(1-\varrho-s)+\sum_{n\geqslant 1}O\bigl(n^{\varrho+\Re s-1-\varepsilon}\bigr). (A.9)

Moreover, each term in the final sum is an entire function in ss, and the OO is uniform for ss in any compact set; thus the sum converges to an analytic function in HεH_{\varepsilon}. Hence, g∗​(s)g^{*}(s) extends to a meromorphic function in HεH_{\varepsilon}, with a single simple pole at s=−ϱs=-\varrho, as asserted.

Let f1​(n):=nϱ​log2​nf_{1}(n):=n^{\varrho}\log_{2}n, and f2​(n):=f⁡(n)−f1​(n)f_{2}(n):=f(n)-f_{1}(n), and let gj:=Λα,β​[fj]g_{j}:=\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[f_{j}], j=1,2j=1,2. We have

and, with ψ⁡(x):=xϱ​log2⁡(x)\psi(x):=x^{\varrho}\log_{2}(x), using the mean-value theorem.

In other words, for all n⩾2n\geqslant 2,

and thus

P^​(k)=P^2​(k)=−Res⁡[f2∗​(s);s=−ϱ−χk].\displaystyle\widehat{P}(k)=\widehat{P}_{2}(k)=-\operatorname{Res}\left[f_{2}^{*}(s);s=-\varrho-\chi_{k}\right]. (A.15)

f1∗​(s)\displaystyle f_{1}^{*}(s) =∑n⩾1∫01f1​(n+t)​(n+t)s−1​𝑑t=∑n⩾1nϱ+s−1​log2​n+∑n⩾1O⁡(nϱ+ℜ⁡s−1−ε)\displaystyle=\sum_{n\geqslant 1}\int_{0}^{1}f_{1}(n+t)(n+t)^{s-1}\,\mathrm{d}t=\sum_{n\geqslant 1}n^{\varrho+s-1}\log_{2}n+\sum_{n\geqslant 1}O\bigl(n^{\varrho+\Re s-1-\varepsilon}\bigr)
=−1log⁡2​ζ′​(1−ϱ−s)+∑n⩾1O⁡(nϱ+ℜ⁡s−1−ε).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\log 2}\zeta^{\prime}(1-\varrho-s)+\sum_{n\geqslant 1}O\bigl(n^{\varrho+\Re s-1-\varepsilon}\bigr). (A.16)

Again, each term in the final sum is an entire function in ss, and the OO is uniform for ss in any compact set; thus the sum converges to an analytic function in HεH_{\varepsilon}. Appendix C Recurrences with minimisation or maximisation

Consider the class of sequences satisfying recurrences of the form

u⁡(n)=min1⩽k⩽⌊n2⌋⁡{α​u​(k)+β​u​(n−k)}(n⩾2),\displaystyle u(n)=\min_{1\leqslant k\leqslant\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor}\left\{\alpha u(k)+\beta u(n-k)\right\}\qquad(n\geqslant 2), (C.1)

with u⁡(1)=1u(1)=1.

This was studied in [5], where it was shown that if α\alpha and β\beta are positive integers with β⩾α\beta\geqslant\alpha, then the minimum in (C.1) is reached at k=⌊n2⌋k=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor and the solution is given by

u⁡(n)=1+(α+β−1)​∑1⩽j<nw⁡(j),u(n)=1+(\alpha+\beta-1)\sum_{1\leqslant j<n}w(j), (C.2)

where

w⁡(j):=αLj−ν0​(j)​βν0​(j),w(j):=\alpha^{L_{j}-\nu_{0}(j)}\beta^{\nu_{0}(j)}, (C.3)

and ν0​(j)\nu_{0}(j) denotes the number of zeros in the binary expansion of jj. We will extend this result and the arguments in [5], and prove the following.

Proposition C.1.

Let α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0 be real numbers such that either

  1. (i)

    β⩾α\beta\geqslant\alpha and β⩾1\beta\geqslant 1, or

  2. (ii)

    α⩾β\alpha\geqslant\beta and α+β⩽1\alpha+\beta\leqslant 1.

Then the minimum in (C.1) is reached at k=⌊n2⌋k=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor. Hence, (C.1) reduces to Λα,β​[u]=0\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[u]=0, and thus (C.1) is solved by u​(n)=Sα,β​(n)u(n)=S_{\alpha,\beta}(n).

Proof.

We note first that Sα,β​(n)S_{\alpha,\beta}(n) is given by the formula in (C.2) for any α,β\alpha,\beta. This follows by (2.44), (2.22), and (2.14) in Section 2, or by the proof in [5].

It thus remains to show that if u⁡(n)u(n) is defined by (C.2), then

α​u​(k)+β​u​(n−k)⩾α​u​(⌊n2⌋)+β​u​(⌈n2⌉)\displaystyle\alpha u(k)+\beta u(n-k)\geqslant\alpha u\bigl({\left\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\right\rfloor}\bigr)+\beta u\bigl({\left\lceil\tfrac{n}{2}\right\rceil}\bigr) (C.4)

for 1⩽k<⌊n2⌋1\leqslant k<\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor. By (C.2), the difference between the two sides of (C.4) is

(α+β−1)​(β​∑⌈n2⌉⩽j<n−kw⁡(j)−α​∑k⩽j<⌊n2⌋w⁡(j)).\displaystyle(\alpha+\beta-1)\left(\beta\sum_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil\leqslant j<n-k}w(j)-\alpha\sum_{k\leqslant j<\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor}w(j)\right). (C.5)

To prove that this is non-negative, we will show that

β​∑⌈n2⌉⩽j<n−kw⁡(j)⩾α​∑k⩽j<⌊n2⌋w⁡(j)\beta\sum_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil\leqslant j<n-k}w(j)\geqslant\alpha\sum_{k\leqslant j<\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor}w(j) (C.6)

if (i) holds, and that (C.6) holds with the inequality reversed if (ii) holds. The key is the following claim:

  1. (a)

    If β⩾α\beta\geqslant\alpha and β⩾1\beta\geqslant 1, then

    β​w​(n+2j)⩾α​w​(n),for all ​n⩾1​ and ​j⩾0.\displaystyle\beta w(n+2^{j})\geqslant\alpha w(n),\quad\text{for all }n\geqslant 1\text{ and }j\geqslant 0. (C.7)
  2. (b)

    If α⩾β\alpha\geqslant\beta and β⩽1\beta\leqslant 1, then

    β​w​(n+2j)⩽α​w​(n),for all ​n⩾1​ and ​j⩾0.\displaystyle\beta w(n+2^{j})\leqslant\alpha w(n),\quad\text{for all }n\geqslant 1\text{ and }j\geqslant 0. (C.8)

Proof of the claim. From (C.3), we have

β​w​(n+2j)α​w​(n)\displaystyle\frac{\beta w(n+2^{j})}{\alpha w(n)} =(βα)1+ν0​(n+2j)−ν0​(n)​αLn+2j−Ln\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)^{1+\nu_{0}(n+2^{j})-\nu_{0}(n)}\alpha^{L_{n+2^{j}}-L_{n}}
=(βα)1+ν0​(n+2j)−ν0​(n)−(Ln+2j−Ln)​βLn+2j−Ln.\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)^{1+\nu_{0}(n+2^{j})-\nu_{0}(n)-(L_{n+2^{j}}-L_{n})}\beta^{L_{n+2^{j}}-L_{n}}. (C.9)

It is easily seen that

1+ν0​(n+2j)−ν0​(n)⩾Ln+2j−Ln⩾0.1+\nu_{0}(n+2^{j})-\nu_{0}(n)\geqslant L_{n+2^{j}}-L_{n}\geqslant 0. (C.10)

Both parts of the claim thus follow from (C.9). ∎

To show (C.6), or its converse in case (ii), which will then complete the proof of the proposition, we combine the claim above with a pairing between the sets, with m:=⌊n2⌋−km:=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor-k,

{⌊n2⌋−m,⋯,⌊n2⌋−1}and{⌈n2⌉,⋯,⌈n2⌉+m−1},\left\{\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor-m,\cdots,\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor-1\right\}\quad\text{and}\quad\left\{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil,\cdots,\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil+m-1\right\}, (C.11)

such that the difference between the elements of each pair is a power of 22. In other words, the proof is completed by applying the following lemma (with a translation). ∎

Lemma C.2.

Let n⩾1n\geqslant 1 and

A\displaystyle A :={1,2,⋯,n},\displaystyle:=\{1,2,\cdots,n\}, (C.12)
C1\displaystyle C_{1} :={n+1,n+2,⋯,2​n},\displaystyle:=\{n+1,n+2,\cdots,2n\}, (C.13)
C2\displaystyle C_{2} :={n+2,n+3,⋯,2​n+1}.\displaystyle:=\{n+2,n+3,\cdots,2n+1\}. (C.14)

There exist one-to-one mappings

h1:A→C1andh2:A→C2,h_{1}:A\rightarrow C_{1}\quad\text{and}\quad h_{2}:A\rightarrow C_{2}, (C.15)

such that for each k∈Ak\in A there exist j1,j2j_{1},j_{2} with

h1​(k)\displaystyle h_{1}(k) =k+2j1,for some ​j1⩾0,\displaystyle=k+2^{j_{1}},\quad\text{for some }j_{1}\geqslant 0, (C.16)
h2​(k)\displaystyle h_{2}(k) =k+2j1,for some ​j2⩾0.\displaystyle=k+2^{j_{1}},\quad\text{for some }j_{2}\geqslant 0. (C.17)
Proof.

We prove the existence of h1h_{1} by induction. Write n=2ℓ+jn=2^{\ell}+j for some ℓ⩾0\ell\geqslant 0 and 0⩽j<2ℓ0\leqslant j<2^{\ell}. (Thus, ℓ=Ln\ell=L_{n}.) We want to show that there exist a one-to-one mapping

h1:{1,⋯,2ℓ+j}→{2ℓ+j+1,⋯,2ℓ+1+2​j},h_{1}:\{1,\cdots,2^{\ell}+j\}\rightarrow\{2^{\ell}+j+1,\cdots,2^{\ell+1}+2j\}, (C.18)

such that for each 1⩽k⩽2ℓ+j1\leqslant k\leqslant 2^{\ell}+j, (C.16) holds.

If j=0j=0, we simply define h1​(k):=k+2ℓh_{1}(k):=k+2^{\ell}.

If j⩾1j\geqslant 1, we first define h1​(k)h_{1}(k) for k⩽2​jk\leqslant 2j by h1​(k):=k+2ℓ+1h_{1}(k):=k+2^{\ell+1}. This gives a mapping from {1,2,⋯,2​j}\{1,2,\cdots,2j\} to {2ℓ+1+1,⋯,2ℓ+1+2​j}\{2^{\ell+1}+1,\cdots,2^{\ell+1}+2j\}. We remove these two blocks, and it remains to define a one-to-one mapping satisfying (C.16) between {2​j+1,⋯,2ℓ+j}\{2j+1,\cdots,2^{\ell}+j\} and {2ℓ+j+1,⋯,2ℓ+1}\{2^{\ell}+j+1,\cdots,2^{\ell+1}\}. By subtracting 2​j2j from each term, it is equivalent to showing that there exist such a mapping from {1,⋯,m}\{1,\cdots,m\} to {m+1,⋯,2​m}\{m+1,\cdots,2m\}, where m=2ℓ−jm=2^{\ell}-j; this is true by the induction hypothesis.

The proof of the existence of h2h_{2} is similar (but with n+1=2ℓ+jn+1=2^{\ell}+j); we omit the details. ∎

If we replace min\min by max\max in (C.1), we obtain a similar result; see also [32] for α>β=1\alpha>\beta=1.

Proposition C.3.

Let α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0 be real numbers such that α⩾β\alpha\geqslant\beta, β⩽1\beta\leqslant 1, and α+β⩾1\alpha+\beta\geqslant 1. Then the maximum in the recursion

u⁡(n)=max1⩽k⩽⌊n2⌋⁡{α​u​(k)+β​u​(n−k)}(n⩾2),\displaystyle u(n)=\max_{1\leqslant k\leqslant\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor}\left\{\alpha u(k)+\beta u(n-k)\right\}\qquad(n\geqslant 2), (C.19)

with u⁡(1)=1u(1)=1, is attained at k=⌊n2⌋k=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor. Hence, (C.19) reduces to Λα,β​[u]=0\Lambda_{\alpha,\beta}[u]=0, and thus (C.19) is solved by u​(n)=Sα,β​(n)u(n)=S_{\alpha,\beta}(n).

Proof.

The proof above shows that under these conditions, (C.8) holds, and hence (C.6) holds in the opposite direction. Thus the difference in (C.5) is ⩽0\leqslant 0. (We do not obtain a second case with α+β<1\alpha+\beta<1; we then would need (C.7), but the condition β⩾1\beta\geqslant 1 in (a) above is incompatible with α+β<1\alpha+\beta<1.) ∎

The results above can be extended to the recurrences of the form

u⁡(n)=min1⩽k⩽⌊n2⌋⁡{α​u​(k)+β​u​(n−k)}+c(n⩾2),\displaystyle u(n)=\min_{1\leqslant k\leqslant\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor}\left\{\alpha u(k)+\beta u(n-k)\right\}+c\qquad(n\geqslant 2), (C.20)

with the same conditions as above on α\alpha and β\beta; see [22, 28] for more general versions. The solution for the recurrence

u⁡(n)=α​u​(⌊n2⌋)+β​u​(⌈n2⌉)+c\displaystyle u(n)=\alpha u\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor\right)+\beta u\left(\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil\right)+c (C.21)

is, with w⁡(j)w(j) as in (C.2)–(C.3) above (see also (4.3))

u⁡(n)=u⁡(1)+((α+β−1)​u​(1)+c)​∑1⩽j<nw⁡(j).u(n)=u(1)+\bigl((\alpha+\beta-1)u(1)+c\bigr)\sum_{1\leqslant j<n}w(j). (C.22)

Appendix D Nowhere differentiability of PA006581​(t)P_{\text{A006581}}(t)

We prove in this appendix the fractal nature of the periodic function P⁡(t)P(t) arising from A006581 (discussed in Example 5.6 with Fourier expansion given in (5.20)), namely, Λ2,2​[f]=g\Lambda_{2,2}[f]=g where g​(n):={n2}​(n−1)g(n):=\{\frac{n}{2}\}(n-1):

f⁡(n)=n2​P​(log2⁡n),\displaystyle f(n)=n^{2}P(\log_{2}n), (D.1)

where, with g¯​(x):=g⁡(x)/x2\bar{g}(x):=g(x)/x^{2},

P⁡(t)=∑m∈ℤ4−m−t​g​(2m+t)=∑m∈ℤg¯​(2m+t).\displaystyle P(t)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}4^{-m-t}g(2^{m+t})=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}\bar{g}(2^{m+t}). (D.2)

Here g⁡(x)g(x) is extended from g⁡(n)g(n) as in (2.2) with φ⁡(t)=t\varphi(t)=t:

g¯​(x)=12​x2×{{x}​⌊x⌋,if ​⌊x⌋​ is even;(1−{x})​(⌊x⌋−1),if ​⌊x⌋​ is odd.\displaystyle\bar{g}(x)=\frac{1}{2x^{2}}\times\begin{cases}\{x\}\lfloor x\rfloor,&\text{if }\lfloor x\rfloor\text{ is even};\\ (1-\{x\})(\lfloor x\rfloor-1),&\text{if }\lfloor x\rfloor\text{ is odd}.\end{cases} (D.3)

Since g¯​(2m+t)=0\bar{g}(2^{m+t})=0 for t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and m⩽0m\leqslant 0, we have

P⁡(t)=∑m⩾1g¯​(2m+t)(0⩽t⩽1).\displaystyle P(t)=\sum_{m\geqslant 1}\bar{g}(2^{m+t})\qquad(0\leqslant t\leqslant 1). (D.4)

The method of proof used here to prove the nowhere differentiability of PP is standard and similar to that for the Takagi function given in the survey paper [1].

Let t∈[0,1)t\in[0,1), and define

τn:=log2⁡⌊2n+t⌋2nandτn′:=log2⁡⌊2n+t⌋+12n.\displaystyle\tau_{n}:=\log_{2}\frac{\lfloor 2^{n+t}\rfloor}{2^{n}}\quad\text{and}\quad\tau_{n}^{\prime}:=\log_{2}\frac{\lfloor 2^{n+t}\rfloor+1}{2^{n}}. (D.5)

To prove that PP does not have a finite derivative at tt, it suffices to show that the sequence

P⁡(τn)−P⁡(τn′)τn−τn′=∑1⩽m⩽ng¯​(2m+τn)−g¯​(2m+τn′)τn−τn′\displaystyle\frac{P(\tau_{n})-P(\tau_{n}^{\prime})}{\tau_{n}-\tau_{n}^{\prime}}=\sum_{1\leqslant m\leqslant n}\frac{\bar{g}(2^{m+\tau_{n}})-\bar{g}(2^{m+\tau_{n}^{\prime}})}{\tau_{n}-\tau_{n}^{\prime}} (D.6)

does not converge to a finite limit. Here we used the relation g¯​(2m+τn)=g¯​(2m+τn′)=0\bar{g}(2^{m+\tau_{n}})=\bar{g}(2^{m+\tau_{n}^{\prime}})=0 for m>nm>n. Now for θ∈[0,1)\theta\in[0,1)

{g¯​(2​k+θ)=k​θ(2​k+θ)2g¯​(2​k+1+θ)=k⁡(1−θ)(2​k+1+θ)2\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} \bar{g}(2k+\theta)&=\frac{k\theta}{(2k+\theta)^{2}}\\ \bar{g}(2k+1+\theta)&=\frac{k(1-\theta)}{(2k+1+\theta)^{2}}\end{aligned}\right. (D.7)

so that, taking the right derivative at integer points here and below,

{g¯′​(2​k+θ)=k⁡(2​k−θ)2​(2​k+θ)3g¯′​(2​k+1+θ)=−k⁡(2​k+3−θ)(2​k+1+θ)3.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} \bar{g}^{\prime}(2k+\theta)&=\frac{k(2k-\theta)}{2(2k+\theta)^{3}}\\ \bar{g}^{\prime}(2k+1+\theta)&=-\frac{k(2k+3-\theta)}{(2k+1+\theta)^{3}}.\end{aligned}\right. (D.8)

If 1⩽m⩽n1\leqslant m\leqslant n, then

⌊2m+τn⌋⩽2m+τn⩽2m+t<2m+τn′⩽⌊2m+τn⌋+1.\displaystyle\lfloor 2^{m+\tau_{n}}\rfloor\leqslant 2^{m+\tau_{n}}\leqslant 2^{m+t}<2^{m+\tau^{\prime}_{n}}\leqslant\lfloor 2^{m+\tau_{n}}\rfloor+1. (D.9)

It follows that h​(x):=g¯​(2x)h(x):=\bar{g}(2^{x}) is infinitely differentiable on [m+τn,m+τn′][m+\tau_{n},m+\tau_{n}^{\prime}], and it is easily seen from (D.8) that h′′​(x)=O​(1)h^{\prime\prime}(x)=O(1) (uniformly in mm and nn). We have, for some τn′′∈(τn,τn′)\tau^{\prime\prime}_{n}\in(\tau_{n},\tau^{\prime}_{n}),

g¯​(2m+τn)−g¯​(2m+τn′)τn−τn′\displaystyle\frac{\bar{g}(2^{m+\tau_{n}})-\bar{g}(2^{m+\tau_{n}^{\prime}})}{\tau_{n}-\tau_{n}^{\prime}} =h⁡(m+τn)−h⁡(m+τn′)τn−τn′=h′​(m+τn′′)\displaystyle=\frac{h(m+\tau_{n})-h(m+\tau_{n}^{\prime})}{\tau_{n}-\tau_{n}^{\prime}}=h^{\prime}(m+\tau^{\prime\prime}_{n})
=h′​(m+t)+O⁡(|τn′′−t|)=h′​(m+t)+O⁡(|τn′−τn|)\displaystyle=h^{\prime}(m+t)+O(|\tau^{\prime\prime}_{n}-t|)=h^{\prime}(m+t)+O(|\tau^{\prime}_{n}-\tau_{n}|)
=h′​(m+t)+O⁡(2−n).\displaystyle=h^{\prime}(m+t)+O(2^{-n}). (D.10)

Hence, (D.6) implies that

P⁡(τn)−P⁡(τn′)τn−τn′=∑1⩽m⩽nh′​(m+t)+O⁡(n​2−n),\displaystyle\frac{P(\tau_{n})-P(\tau_{n}^{\prime})}{\tau_{n}-\tau_{n}^{\prime}}=\sum_{1\leqslant m\leqslant n}h^{\prime}(m+t)+O(n2^{-n}), (D.11)

and thus, if PP is differentiable at tt, then the sum

∑m⩾1h′​(m+t)\displaystyle\sum_{m\geqslant 1}h^{\prime}(m+t) (D.12)

converges (and equals P′​(t)P^{\prime}(t)).

On the other hand, it follows easily from (D.8) that if x⩾2x\geqslant 2, then x​g¯′​(x)⩾19x\bar{g}^{\prime}(x)\geqslant\frac{1}{9} for even ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor and x​g¯′​(x)⩽−14x\bar{g}^{\prime}(x)\leqslant-\frac{1}{4} for odd ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor. Hence, |h′​(m+t)|=|2m+t​g¯′​(2m+t)​log⁡2|⩾log⁡29|h^{\prime}(m+t)|=|2^{m+t}\bar{g}^{\prime}(2^{m+t})\log 2|\geqslant\frac{\log 2}{9} for all m⩾1m\geqslant 1. Consequently, the sum (D.12) diverges for any tt, and thus PP is nowhere differentiable.

Moreover, we note that if 2t2^{t} is a dyadic rational, then for all large mm, 2m+t2^{m+t} is an even integer, and thus h′​(m+t)⩾log⁡29h^{\prime}(m+t)\geqslant\frac{\log 2}{9}. Hence, in this case the sum (D.12) diverges to +∞+\infty, and thus so does (P⁡(τn)−P⁡(τn′))/(τn−τn′)\bigl(P(\tau_{n})-P(\tau^{\prime}_{n})\bigr)/(\tau_{n}-\tau^{\prime}_{n}) in (D.6); consequently, PP is not Lipschitz.

We do not know whether PP is Hölder continuous, and leave that as an open problem. Note that Lemma 3.4 does not apply since (3.10) does not hold.
